VI. Paul’s Divinely Given Task and His Suffering for the Gentiles (3:1–13)

A. Paul’s Role in the Administration of the Mystery (3:1–7)

B. How Paul Fulfills His Task (3:8–13)


A. Paul’s Role in the Administration of the Mystery (3:1–7)

Paul begins 3:1–13 with an emphatic self-reference to his imprisonment (ἐγὼ Παῦλος ὁ δέσμιος, egō Paulos ho desmios, I, Paul, the prisoner). The pathos of this reference seems to be an appropriate introduction to a prayer whose subject is his readers’ understanding of the limitless love of Christ (vv. 14–19). Mention of his imprisonment on behalf of his Gentile readers then leads Paul into a sustained reflection on the responsibility he bears as a recipient of divine revelation about God’s purposes for the Gentiles (vv. 2–13). Perhaps at some level Paul is answering in 3:2–7 the question implied in 3:1 of why he is in prison for the Gentiles.

The first part of the digression (vv. 2–7) describes the close link between Paul’s “responsibility of administering” (οἰκονομία, oikonomia) the task God has given him and “the mystery” God has revealed to him. Paul describes this link in three successive phases. First, he tells his readers how he knows and understands the mystery: it came to him by means of a divine revelation (vv. 3–4). Second, he asserts that the mystery was utterly unknown until the Spirit revealed it to Christ’s holy apostles and to prophets (v. 5).

Third, he gives the content of the mystery as the union in one body, on fully equal terms, of Jewish and Gentile believers through the gospel (v. 6). This description of the mystery differs from the description of it in 1:9–10, where the term last occurred. There the mystery was more broadly conceived as the summation of all things, whether in heaven or on earth, in Christ. Here the mystery is one part of that grand scheme—the unification of two formerly separated ethnic groups in one body through the gospel. The reason for this narrowed focus probably lies in the purpose of the digression. Paul is describing his own administrative responsibility (οἰκονομία; 3:3) in God’s administration (οἰκονομία; 1:10) of this all-encompassing plan, and Paul’s role is focused on bringing Gentile believers into the newly constituted people of God.

Throughout the passage an important subtheme is the grace of God. Paul was not given the important responsibility he describes here, with its special insight and understanding into the previously unknown mystery, because of any qualifications of his own. His explanation of the link between his responsibility and the mystery is sandwiched between descriptions of his task as “the grace of God given to me” (v. 2) and “the gift of God’s grace given to me” (v. 7a), and the passage ends with the statement that Paul became a “servant” of the gospel only by means of the effective working of God’s power (v. 7b). This theme provides a link to the next section, which opens with an emphatic reference to Paul as “the least of all the saints” and again describes his task as the “grace . . . given” to him (v. 8).

The passage is thoughtfully articulated. Not only does its end correspond to its beginning and provide a smooth transition to the next long sentence, but it also skillfully picks up the language of the previous section. The three συν- words in 3:6 echo the three συν- words of 2:19–22,﻿[1] and the critical term οἰκονομία in 3:2 picks up the six -οἰκ- words of 2:19–22.﻿[2]

Still, the passage bears signs of extemporaneity. The false start in 3:1, the pathos of Paul’s first-person reference to his imprisonment in that same verse (“I Paul, the prisoner”), the lack of an object for the three prefixed prepositions in 3:6 (“heirs together and one body together and sharers in the promise together with” . . . whom?), and the sheer length of the sentence itself (105 words)—these all look like a communication that was actually dictated with some emotion. On a smaller scale it is reminiscent of 2 Cor. 2:14–7:4, where Paul’s narrative of the geographical and temporal details of his turbulent relationship with the Corinthians (1:12–2:13) prompted him to digress in 2:14–7:4 on the nature of his often-difficult ministry of the Spirit and righteousness. He then returned in 7:5, with a repetition of the language of 2:13, to the details he had left behind.[3] Similarly, here in Ephesians a reference to his suffering in the cause of the gospel in 3:1 prompts a reflection on his apostolic responsibility. When he finally returns to his original train of thought in 3:14, he signals this return with a repetition of the language he was using when he began to digress (τούτου χάριν, toutou charin).

As the exegesis brings out, 3:1–7 presents some significant challenges to those who think Ephesians is a genuine Pauline letter. These signs of extemporaneity, pathos, and Paul’s normal mode of discourse, however, look genuine. It would have been possible to fake such elements, but it seems more likely that Paul himself was moved to speak this way as his secretary furiously took down his words.



Exegesis and Exposition

1For this reason, I, Paul, the prisoner of Christ ⌜ ⌝ for you Gentiles—2if, as I assume, you have heard about the responsibility of administering the grace of God given to me for you, 3⌜that⌝ the mystery was made known to me by revelation, just as I wrote briefly above, 4according to which, when you read, you are able to perceive my insight into the mystery of Christ, 5which was not made known to the sons of human beings in other generations as it has now been revealed by the Spirit to his holy apostles, and prophets, 6that the Gentiles are heirs together and one body together and sharers in the promise together with [Jewish believers] in Christ Jesus, through the gospel, 7of which I became a servant according to the gift of God’s grace given to me according to the effect of his power.

[3:1] Paul begins his prayer with τούτου χάριν (toutou charin, for this reason), a phrase that can point either backward to what has been said (e.g., 1 Macc. 12:45; 13:4) or forward to something that will be said (e.g., Titus 1:5; Philo, Joseph 45; Dio Chrysostom, Or. 35.2). Here it probably does not refer forward to the substance of Paul’s prayer report (3:16–19) but backward to what Paul has just said about the incorporation of Gentile believers, alongside Jewish believers, into the metaphorical dwelling place of God (2:19–22; cf. Ellicott 1859: 56; Haupt 1902a: 95; Lincoln 1990: 172). “For this reason,” Paul the prisoner prays that his Gentile readers will grasp the vastness of Christ’s love (3:16–19). Paul’s knowledge of what God has done for his Gentile readers in Christ (2:19–22) prompts him to pray that they too will understand the vastness of the love that God has shown for them in Christ (3:14–19).

This prayerful concern for his readers arose from Paul’s special role as an apostle to the Gentiles. As their apostle, he felt a strong responsibility not only to proclaim the gospel to them but also to nurture them in the faith so that they might persevere to the end. His reference to himself as ἐγὼ Παῦλος (egō Paulos, I, Paul) probably reflects these convictions. Paul uses this expression elsewhere when he wants to defend or emphasize his apostleship to the Gentiles (Gal. 5:2; 2 Cor. 10:1; Col. 1:23) or when he wants to express his deep concern for those who have believed the gospel through his preaching (1 Thess. 2:18).[4] Here these concerns coalesce: Paul wanted to help his discouraged readers with his prayer (3:13), and he wanted to do this precisely because he was an apostle to the Gentiles.

Paul describes himself not as an apostle, however, but as ὁ δέσμιος (ho desmios, the prisoner). The article places special emphasis on his imprisonment, and the mention of his imprisonment was probably intended to add pathos and conviction to his prayer: those who go to prison for what they believe are worth hearing (cf. 6:20; Philem. 1, 9; 2 Tim. 1:8; Rev. 1:9).[5] Paul is not a prisoner of Rome but τοῦ Χριστου (tou Christou, of Christ) and ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν τῶν ἐθνῶν (hyper hymōn tōn ethnōn, for you Gentiles). He may have been thinking here of how Christ chose him to bear the burden (βαστάζω, bastazō) of his name before the Gentiles and to suffer much in the process (Acts 9:15–16; cf. Luke 14:27). An analogy between his own suffering in this way “for” the salvation of the Gentiles and the suffering of Christ “for” others is explicitly expressed in Col. 1:24 and may also lie behind his use of ὑπέρ (hyper) both here and later in 3:13 (BDAG 1030; cf., e.g., 5:25; 2 Cor. 12:15; Mark 14:24).[6]

[3:2] Mention of his imprisonment in order to bring the gospel to the Gentiles has prompted Paul to digress on the origin and nature of his special role in this task. He begins with a combination of particles (εἴ γε, ei ge) that appears only five times in the NT: once here, once in 4:21, and three other times, all in the Pauline corpus (Gal. 3:4; 2 Cor. 5:3; Col. 1:23). According to Denniston (1954: 114–15), “the essential force” of the particle γε (ge) “appears to be concentration,” but it expresses this emphasis so delicately that it should be “rendered in English by an inflexion of the voice, or by italics” rather than by words (cf. Smyth §§2821, 2823).

Such a fine nuance inevitably makes the phrase εἴ γε ambiguous: it can imply either doubt or certainty (Moule 1959: 164), and sometimes the decision about which of these is in view is difficult (2 Cor. 5:3; Col. 1:23). Here, oddly, there is an element of both meanings: Paul has no real doubt that his readers have heard of him, any more than he doubts that they have heard about Jesus when he uses the expression again in 4:20–21 (Thrall 1962: 88). At the same time, the γε reveals some personal distance between Paul and his readers: “If, as I assume, you have heard” (cf., e.g., Abbott 1897: 78; MacDonald 2000: 261). This distance is sometimes attributed to a pseudonymous author writing in a general way to a wide audience who, he is “sure,” has heard of the famous apostle’s vocation (e.g., Lincoln 1990: 173). If so, the emotion expressed by both the broken syntax and the phrase ἐγὼ Παῦλος ὁ δέσμιος in 3:1–2 seems extremely artificial. This is certainly possible—ancient forgers sometimes worked with surprising subtlety (cf. “Plato,” Ep. 12; Donelson 1986: 25–26)—but it is at least equally likely that these elements are evidence that the real Paul dictated this letter (perhaps quickly and with some emotion) and that the εἴ γε reveals his intention that a wide audience of believers in Ephesus should read it or hear it read. After Paul’s absence from the city for over seven years, nearly five of them in various forms of imprisonment, many of these intended readers would have had only a loose connection to him.[7]

Paul assumes that his audience has heard about τὴν οἰκονομίαν τῆς χάριτος τοῦ θεοῦ τῆς δοθείσης μοι εἰς ὑμᾶς (tēn oikonomian tēs charitos tou theou tēs dotheisēs moi eis hymas, the responsibility of administering the grace of God given to me for you). The term οἰκονομία can refer to a “plan” that is administered, to the task of “administration,” or to the responsibility of an administrator, and interpreters differ about which of these meanings is most suitable here. In 3:9 the word refers to the “administrative plan” God has now revealed (cf. Ign. Eph. 18.2), and if we import that meaning here, then Paul might be speaking of God’s plan to use him to preach the gospel to the Gentiles, a plan that either originated with God’s grace or had grace “as its characteristic element” (Eadie 1883: 213; cf., e.g., Robinson 1904: 167; Gnilka 1971: 163; Schnackenburg 1991: 131; Best 1998: 298–99).[8]

Elsewhere in Paul’s Letters, however, the term refers to either the responsibility or the task of administering something, and sometimes it is difficult to distinguish between these two nuances.[9] In Eph. 1:10 it refers to God’s task of administering the fullness of the times (see the comments on that verse). In 1 Cor. 9:16–17 and Col. 1:25, it could be understood either as Paul’s task of preaching the gospel or as the responsibility given to him to be such a preacher. Here in Eph. 3:2, however, the distinction between the two nuances is clearer. The “grace” that Paul administers is his God-given task of preaching the gospel to the Gentiles (cf. v. 7, and see below), and that leaves οἰκονομία to refer to the responsibility that God has given to him to accomplish this task.[10] Paul assumes that his special responsibility of administering the grace of God to Gentiles is well known to his believing Gentile readers.

The translation “responsibility of administering,” however, fails to show the connection between οἰκονομία and the many -οἰκ- (-oik-) terms in 2:19–22.[11] Indeed, the primary meaning of οἰκονομία in Paul’s time was “management of a household” (LSJ 1204; L. Johnson 2001: 148–49), and the connection was probably lost on neither Paul nor his readers (cf. Eadie 1883: 213). God has given him the responsibility of administering the part of his plan for the universe that involves the inclusion of the Gentiles within his household.[12]

Paul refers to the task for which he is responsible in an unusual way. It is, he says, “the grace [χάρις, charis] of God given to me for you [Gentiles].” Up to this point Paul has used the term χάρις as the central characteristic of salvation: God gives salvation freely, generously, and at great cost to the most undeserving of people (1:6–7; 2:5, 7–8). Here in 3:2, however, Paul uses the term in the way he will use it in 3:7–8, as the hallmark of his own vocation of preaching the gospel to the Gentiles. God did not simply give him the gospel message of grace to take to the Gentiles, but the assignment to do this is itself, in a special sense, God’s grace given to Paul (τῆς δοθείσης μοι, tēs dotheisēs moi; cf. vv. 7 and 8). The idea that the task God has given Paul is a demonstration of God’s grace appears often in Paul’s Letters (Gal. 2:7–9; 1 Cor. 3:10; 15:10; Phil. 1:7; Rom. 1:5; 12:3; 15:15), and in 4:7 he will use χάρις this way of all believers when he says that “to each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of the gift of Christ.”[13]

Paul’s reference to himself as “the least of all the saints” in 3:8 probably shows us the link between these two uses of the term “grace.” God’s willingness to use Paul to preach the gospel among the Gentiles was a signal demonstration of his grace (3:7; cf. Gal. 1:13–16; 1 Cor. 15:9–10; 1 Tim. 1:12–16). Just as in salvation generally, God’s grace is evident in his desire to save those who are dead in trespasses and sins, so with Paul specifically, God’s grace is evident in his use of a former persecutor of the church, and zealot for an exclusivist form of Jewish tradition, to preach the good news that the Gentiles are now included among God’s people.

[3:3] Paul next defines the administrative responsibility God has given to him more specifically.[14] As the parallel between “to me” (μοι, moi) in 3:2 and “to me” (μοι, moi) here demonstrates, the critical role God has graciously given to Paul (v. 2) is intimately tied to the revelation to Paul of the “mystery” (μυστήριον, mystērion). It is only because God has revealed the mystery to him that he has a responsibility and a divinely given task to fulfill.

Paul has received this part of the mystery, he says, κατὰ ἀποκάλυψιν (kata apocalypsin). This phrase does not refer to the “norm” or “ground” according to which the mystery was made known, as if the revelation of the mystery to Paul followed a certain previously conceived pattern (pace Lincoln 1990: 175; BDAG 512). It instead refers to the means by which the mystery was made known to Paul: it came to him “by revelation” from God.[15] In Dan. 2:17–19 Daniel received information about both the content and the interpretation of Nebuchadnezzar’s dream apart from any cleverness of his own, and strictly because God in his mercy revealed it to him (thus saving his life). Similarly, Paul received his insight into the part of the mystery that was of particular relevance to the Gentiles only “by revelation” from God (cf. δι᾿ ἀποκαλύψεως, di’ apokalypseōs, in Gal. 1:12) and as an act of God’s mercy (1 Tim. 1:13). No amount of exegetical study of the Scriptures would have yielded this insight; God had to make it known to Paul personally (vv. 5, 9; Best 1997a: 121; 1998: 300).

The content of this divine revelation, Paul says next, is not something new to the readers. He has written about it briefly before (καθὼς προέγραψα ἐν ὀλίγῳ, kathōs proegrapsa en oligō, just as I wrote briefly above). The phrase ἐν ὀλίγῳ (en oligō) is a common expression for “in brief” (BDAG 703) or “within a small compass” (LSJ 1215), but the term προγράφω (prographō) is more ambiguous. It can refer to something written a long time “beforehand,” such as the Scriptures (Rom. 15:4; Jude 4), or to something that was written “above” in the same document (LSJ 1473; BDAG 867). Down through the years some interpreters have thought that the reference was to some other communication of Paul (Chrysostom, Hom. Eph., hom. 6; NPNF 13:76; Calvin 1965: 158), perhaps a ten-letter collection of his letters to which our Ephesians formed a pseudepigraphic introduction (Goodspeed 1951: 287–88), perhaps to Colossians (Muddiman 2001: 151–52), or perhaps to a specific passage in a Pauline letter, such as Gal. 1:15–16 (Sellin 2008: 251). Others believe it refers to the mention of the mystery in 1:9 (Alford 1857: 100). However, Paul is probably describing what he has just written about the unity of Jews and Gentiles in Christ in 2:11–22 (Theodoret [R. Hill 2001: 2.42]; Haupt 1902a: 98n1; Masson 1953: 173; Schnackenburg 1991: 132). He may be thinking even more specifically of the language of inclusion in 2:19–22 with its συν- compounds (cf. 3:6).

[3:4] Πρός (pros) can occasionally be used with the accusative case to mean “according to” (BDAG 875; 2 Esd. 6:13 LXX [Ezra 6:13 MT, Eng.]; Wis. 16:21; Gal. 2:14; 2 Cor. 5:10; Herm. Sim. 9.5.2), and that is apparently how Paul uses it here in the phrase πρὸς ὅ (pros ho).[16] What he has written beforehand (perhaps specifically in 2:19–22) provides evidence “according to which” his readers are able to perceive that he has insight into the mystery of Christ.

This perception will come ἀναγινώσκοντες (anaginōskontes), “when [they] read.” It was normal in antiquity to read aloud, even when reading privately, but here Paul has in mind the public reading of the letter.[17] Thus, he is not imagining that they will now back up and study what he has written before this point,[18] but he is simply thinking from his own perspective as the letter’s author that when they hear read aloud what he has just written, they will appreciate the insight God has given him.[19]

The term σύνεσις (synesis, insight) refers to understanding not that Paul himself has ingeniously developed, but that has been given to him by God (cf. Exod. 31:3 LXX; 35:1 LXX; Sir. 1:19 LXX; Col. 1:9; 2:2). This is clear from 3:2, where Paul’s critical role is attributed to the grace given to him, and from his statement in 3:3 that his knowledge of the mystery has been made known to him by revelation. Both δοθείσης (dotheisēs, given, v. 2) and ἐγνωρίσθη (egnōristhē, made known, v. 3) are divine passives. The source of his insight, then, is God, and this rescues the reference to “my insight” here in 3:4 from any element of boasting or egotism (cf. Best 1998: 304).

Some scholars have taken the reference to Paul’s own insight to be a clear sign that the letter comes from a post-Pauline author who wanted to boost the apostle’s authority after his death (e.g., Gnilka 1971: 165; Lincoln 1990: 176; cf. Baur 2003: 2.33; Sterling 2008: 87–88). Lincoln, for example, argues that although Paul commends himself in the undisputed letters, he does this only in polemical settings (Gal. 1–2; 1 Cor. 14:37–38; 2 Cor. 10–13). The “unprovoked and unqualified” character of the reference to Paul’s insight here in Ephesians sets it apart from those other instances (Lincoln 1990: 176; cf. Gnilka 1971: 165).

First-person claims of special insight frequently appear in Jewish apocalyptic literature, however, and since the language of revelation is so prominent in Eph. 3:2–3, this seems to be the most likely cultural context in which to understand the first-person references here (Aletti 2001: 177).[20] If so, then the claims are probably not an attempt to boost Paul’s waning authority since this is not the function of such claims in the apocalyptic literature from the Second Temple period and shortly thereafter. First-person claims of special insight appear both in pseudepigraphic documents (2 Esd. [4 Ezra] 5:22; 14:40; T. Levi 2.3; 2 Bar. 81.4) and in the Qumran Hymns (1QHa 10.13; 20.13), which are anonymous but not pseudepigraphic. In both contexts their purpose seems to be to assure the reader that the insight of the seer is from God, not that the seer himself has any special authority (Aletti 2001: 177). The claim of special insight here in 3:4, therefore, probably should not be read as weighty evidence either for or against authenticity, and in any case, the argument should not hinge on how likely Paul would be to commend himself as a possessor of special insight.

The content of Paul’s insight—what he has insight “into” (cf. 2 Tim. 2:7; BDAG 970)—is τὸ μυστήριον τοῦ Χριστοῦ (to mystērion tou Christou, the mystery of Christ). This could mean “the mystery that is Christ,” an idea that some interpreters believe lies behind Col. 1:27 (τὸ μυστήριον . . . , ὅ ἐστιν Χριστὸς ἐν ὑμῖν, to mystērion . . . , ho estin Christos en hymin, the mystery . . . , which is Christ in you).[21] It is more likely, however, that Paul refers to “the mystery about Christ.”[22] In light of Paul’s coming definition of the mystery as the close bond across ethnic lines between all Christians (v. 6), he is probably thinking here of the leading role that Christ plays in bringing unity to believers, according to 2:14–22.

[3:5] This mystery, Paul says next, “was not made known . . . in other generations,” a comment that has raised more than a few eyebrows over the years.[23] As Paul will clarify shortly, the mystery is the full inclusion of the Gentiles into the people of God by means of their faith in the gospel and their incorporation into Christ, which results from this (v. 6). Yet it is difficult to see this inclusion as something completely unanticipated “in other generations.” Both the OT and noncanonical Jewish literature from the Second Temple period (and shortly thereafter) attest a lively expectation of the Gentiles’ inclusion in the worship of God at the time of Israel’s eschatological restoration.[24]

One very early approach to the problem claims that Paul speaks in relative terms: the inclusion of the Gentiles was known theoretically (Theodoret [R. Hill 2001: 2.42]; cf. Origen [Heine 2002: 145–46]; Barth 1974: 334n45), or vaguely (Theophylact, PG 124:1069; Calvin 1965: 160; Robinson 1928: 73), or to comparatively few (Eadie 1883: 217; Muddiman 2001: 154) in ancient times but now has become a reality, or become clear, or become known to many. Exegetical backing for this interpretation is sometimes sought in the phrase τοῖς υἱοῖς τῶν ἀνθρώπων (tois huiois tōn anthrōpōn, to the sons of human beings) which, it is said, may refer to common people generally as opposed to the special class of patriarchs and prophets who knew about the mystery (Eadie 1883: 217).[25] More often, commentators interpret the ὡς (ōs, as) that follows this phrase as comparative and as therefore indicating that the mystery was not made known to people in previous generations to the same degree that it has now been made known (Theodoret [R. Hill 2001: 2.42]; Alford 1857: 101; Ellicott 1859: 59; Eadie 1883: 217; Abbott 1897: 82; Westcott 1906: 45; cf. Chrysostom, Hom. Eph., hom. 6; NPNF 13:76–77).

More recent interpreters, however, are almost united in rejecting this approach, and they are probably correct to do so.[26] In the next paragraph, Paul will go over much the same ground again and will express himself unambiguously: the mystery now revealed to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places was hidden for ages past in the God who created the world (3:9–10; cf. Col. 1:26; Aletti 2001: 178; Grindheim 2003: 534). The mystery, therefore, was wholly unknown in the past and has now been revealed. Before deciding that the author has expressed himself in a way that is inconsistent with his affirmation of the OT elsewhere in the letter (Barth 1974: 334; cf. Best 1998: 306) or that is inconsistent with the perspective on the OT in the undisputed Paulines (Lincoln 1982: 47; 1990: 178), however, it is necessary to decide precisely what Paul considers the mystery to be in this context.

In 3:6 Paul will identify the mystery as the full inclusion of Gentile believers within the people of God. They are, he says, συγκληρονόμα καὶ σύσσωμα καὶ συμμέτοχα τῆς ἐπαγγελίας (synklēronoma kai syssōma kai symmetocha tēs epangelias, heirs together and one body together and sharers in the promise together) with Jewish Christians. The words compounded with the preposition συν- (syn-, together) recall the terms συμπολῖται (sympolitai, citizens together), συναρμολογουμένη (synarmologoumenē, being joined together), and συνοικοδομεῖσθε (synoikodomeisthe, you are being built together) in the preceding paragraph (2:19, 21, 22), with its focus on the complete unity of Jewish and Gentile believers and on their common function as building blocks in the metaphorical building that is becoming the dwelling place of God. The mystery, then, is not merely the unity of Jews and Gentiles in the worship of the one God but their equality with each other (2:11–12).

The equality of Jews with Gentiles in the eschatological period of Israel’s restoration is not easy to infer from either the OT or the Jewish literature of the period. Without the clarifying lens of the gospel, some OT passages could be misunderstood to mean that the Gentiles would serve Israel during the time of its restoration (e.g., Isa. 45:14; 60:1–16; Hag. 2:7; Ps. 68:29, 31; cf. 1QM 12.13–15; Tob. 13:11; Pss. Sol. 17.30; Jeremias 1982: 58–61). The mystery long unknown to people in other generations and now revealed, therefore, is that in Christ Jesus and through the gospel, Gentile Christians are fully equal members of the people of God with Jewish Christians. Paul may also have in mind, as Grindheim (2003: 531–53) has convincingly argued, the achievement of this unity by means of setting aside the Mosaic law (2:14–15), a development that was certainly unanticipated in any known form of pre-Christian Jewish expectation.

This mystery, Paul says, νῦν ἀπεκαλύφθη τοῖς ἁγίοις ἀποστόλοις αὐτοῦ καὶ προφήταις ἐν πνεύματι (nyn apekalyphthē tois hagiois apostolois autou kai prophētais en pneumati, has now been revealed by the Spirit to his holy apostles and prophets). This statement has received close scrutiny both because its syntax is unclear and because its character is unusual.

At the level of syntax, there are three principal questions: First, does Paul intend the terms ἁγίοις (hagiois, holy) and αὐτοῦ (autou, his) to describe only ἀποστόλοις (apostolois, apostles), or does he mean for them to apply also to προφήταις (prophētais, prophets)? Second, does αὐτοῦ in this phrase refer to Christ or to God? Third, does ἐν πνεύματι (en pneumati, in the Spirit) modify προφήταις or the verb ἀπεκαλύφθη (apekalyphthē, was revealed)?

In answer to the first question, interpreters often observe that the concept of “holy prophets” is not uncommon in Christian literature from the period (Luke 1:70; Acts 3:21; 2 Pet. 3:2) and that the single article binds apostles and prophets together so that any modifiers are likely to apply to both. Thus, we should translate “his holy apostles and prophets” and see both “his” and “holy” as qualifying both “prophets” and “apostles” (Schlier 1957: 150; Best 1998: 307; Hoehner 2002: 442–43).

It is true that the single article binds “apostles” closely with “prophets,” something we would expect from their common, foundational function in 2:20. Nevertheless, the way Paul has sandwiched ἀποστόλοις between ἁγίοις and αὐτοῦ and placed the whole three-word unit before the καί (kai, and) probably means that he wants to draw a distinction between apostles and prophets (Schnackenburg 1991: 133–34; O’Brien 1999: 233; cf. Lincoln 1990: 179). Paul intends, therefore, to refer to “his holy apostles, and prophets.” If this reading is correct, then it would be consistent with the distinction that Paul seems to make between apostles and prophets in 4:11, where he sees them as two separate groups and probably lists apostles first because of their primary importance (ἔδωκεν τοὺς μὲν ἀποστόλους, τοὺς δὲ προφήτας, edōken tous men apostolous, tous de prophētas, and he gave some to be apostles, others to be prophets).

Why do they have this place of primacy? Although a connection with the historical Jesus was not, in Paul’s thinking, an absolutely necessary qualification for an apostle,[27] it seems to have been a characteristic of most apostles, including the last and least of these—Paul himself (1 Cor. 9:1; 15:7–9). This link with the historical Jesus and therefore with the events that precipitated the dramatic change that Paul describes in 3:5 probably sets the apostles apart in Paul’s mind from all other Christians as critically important to the church’s identity. This is why he calls them “holy.”

The correlation between 3:5 and 4:11 also helps us to answer the second question: To whom does αὐτοῦ refer? Despite the claim of some commentators that the αὐτοῦ refers to God (cf. Col. 1:26), its antecedent is more likely to be Christ. He gives the gift of apostleship in 4:11, and his explicit appearance at the end of 3:4 means that a reference to him is most natural.[28]

Some commentators have also decided that distinguishing between “apostles” and “prophets” helps to answer the third question: What does ἐν πνεύματι modify? If we take “holy” with “apostles,” they argue, perhaps we should take ἐν πνεύματι with “prophets.” Each term would then have its own modifier (Schnackenburg 1991: 133–34; Pokorný 1992: 143; cf. Eadie 1883: 218–19; Schlier 1957: 150). It is more likely, however, that ἐν πνεύματι goes with the verb ἀπεκαλύφθη to describe how the revelation took place. In 1 Cor. 2:6–10, a passage with close verbal and conceptual links to Eph. 3:2–13, Paul explicitly says that God “revealed” (ἀπεκάλυψεν, apekalypsen) his “wisdom in a mystery” (σοφία ἐν μυστηρίῳ, sophia en mysteriō) “through the Spirit” (διὰ τοῦ πνεύματος, dia tou pneumatos) to those who proclaim the gospel.[29] This makes it likely that here too Paul intends to speak of the Spirit as the one through whom the revelation was given (Fee 1994: 692; pace Heil 2007b: 512–13).[30]

If these syntactical decisions are correct, then the text describes the mystery about Christ, which, it says, was unknown in former times but was revealed by the Spirit to two distinct groups: the holy apostles of Christ and the prophets. This way of putting things, however, raises two critical questions.

The first question is whether it is likely that the same Paul, who in the undisputed letters applies the term “holy” to all Christians, would now use this term to separate the apostles from other Christians and then speak of them as a special group within the people of God. Scholars who believe that Ephesians is pseudonymous tend to give a negative answer to this question.[31] Not only is this the only appearance in the NT of the phrase “holy apostles,” but where the adjective ἅγιος (hagios, holy) is used substantively in the Pauline corpus, it most often, and perhaps always, refers to Christians generally.[32] In addition, if the author of Ephesians has relied on Colossians, then he seems to have transformed a reference in Col. 1:26 to “his saints,” meaning all God’s people, into a reference to “his holy apostles and prophets,” meaning those foundational witnesses of the past to whom God originally communicated the mystery.[33] Such a move would be consistent with a tendency that many scholars identify in the development of early Christianity toward emphasizing the role of the earliest Christian “apostles and prophets” as the foundation of the church (cf. 2:20).[34]

Several commentators mention that the phrase “holy apostles” is similar to the use of “holy elders” for church leaders in Ignatius (Magn. 3.1).[35] Ephesians, then, seems to participate in the subapostolic tendency to dignify special titles (such as “elder” or “apostle”) with this adjective (“holy”). We could perhaps add to this the tendency in the late first and early second centuries to use commendatory adjectives of important Christians of the past (e.g., Ign. Eph. 12.2; 1 Clem. 5.2; 47.1; Pol. Phil. 3.2; 11.3).

This is a strong argument, but for two reasons it is not decisive. First, it is not entirely clear that when the Paul of the undisputed letters uses the term ἅγιοι as a substantive, as he does in Col. 1:26, he is always referring to God’s people as a whole rather than to a special group within it. Scholars have long recognized this possibility with respect to the Jerusalem “saints” for whom Paul intended the collection he took up among his predominantly Gentile churches (1 Cor. 16:1; 2 Cor. 8:4; 9:12), and Bockmuehl (1990: 184–85) has argued persuasively that ἅγιοι in Col. 1:26 may also refer to a particular group of Christians. Although Bockmuehl (1990: 201) acknowledges some “ambivalence” in the expression, he points out that taking ἅγιοι here as a special group fits the evidence in several ways. It is consistent, he argues, with Paul’s contention that he, Apollos, and Cephas, among others, have a special role as the recipients and administrators of God’s mysteries (1 Cor. 2:1, 10; 4:1–2). It also preserves the distinction, implicit in Col. 1:27–28, between those such as Paul, who communicate the mystery, and those such as the Gentiles and the Colossians in particular, to whom they communicate it.

If the “saints” of Col. 1:26 are a special group who proclaim the mystery, however, then Eph. 3:5 merely names this group more specifically as “his holy apostles, and prophets.” It does not betray a conceptual development that goes beyond the understanding articulated either in the undisputed letters or in Colossians (cf. Percy 1946: 346–47).

Second, it is important to nuance the argument that the designation “his holy apostles” breathes the air of a later time. This argument has changed little since the mid-nineteenth century when Baur (2003: 2.32) claimed that Eph. 3:5 was an example of how reverence toward figures in the apostolic age increased with the passing of time. Yet this claim needs to be balanced with evidence from the earliest extant Christian literature that leaders of the first generation were already highly esteemed and given titles of dignity. In 1 Thess. 5:12–13, Paul urges his readers to “esteem [their leaders] very highly” (ἡγεῖσθαι αὐτοὺς ὑπερεκπερισσοῦ, hēgeisthai autous hyperekperissou). In Gal. 2:9 we learn that the Jerusalem church referred to James, Peter, and John as “the pillars,” perhaps borrowing a traditional Jewish title of honor (cf. 1 Clem. 5.2; Betz 1979: 99n404; Martyn 1997: 205). Speaking of the apostles as “holy” would not move us into a completely different conceptual world, although the precise language is, without question, unusual for Paul (Dahl 2000: 54).

Who are these “holy apostles and prophets”? They must be identical to the “apostles and prophets” who form the foundation of God’s variegated dwelling place—a temple whose building blocks are believers from among both Jews and Gentiles (2:20–22). They are, then, people such as Peter, Barnabas, Apollos, and certainly Paul himself, who presided over the extension of the gospel to the Gentiles (Percy 1946: 346–49; cf. Gal. 2:7, 9; 1 Cor. 3:5–6, 22; 4:6, 9; 9:5–6; Acts 13:1–3; 14:4, 14; 15:22, 32).

This leads to the second major critical question raised by this passage: Why does Paul emphasize the centrality of his own role in receiving and communicating the mystery in 3:2–4 and 8–10 but here in 3:5 claim that the apostles and prophets generally have that role?

According to some who think Ephesians is pseudonymous, the passage represents the confluence of two contradictory streams of early Christian tradition about how the gospel first advanced to the Gentiles (Best 1997a: 103–38; Sterling 2008: 88; cf. Lincoln 1990: 179–80). One stream is present in the four canonical Gospels and Acts and depicts the twelve apostles as recipients of a commission to preach the gospel to the Gentiles.[36] Perhaps its chronologically earliest appearance in the extant literature, however, is here in Eph. 3:5. The other stream is present in both the disputed and undisputed Pauline correspondence, and it is detectable in one brief sentence in Acts.[37] This stream identifies Paul as the last of the apostles and uniquely commissioned among this group to take the gospel to the Gentiles. This tradition appears in Eph. 3:3 and 3:8 and stands in conflict with the tradition in 3:5. “Probably,” says Best (1997a: 132), “the author of Ephesians had not thought this problem through.”

It seems more likely, however, that Eph. 3:1–13 reflects the complexity of the actual situation in the early days of the church’s mission. This complexity appears with the same contours in Paul’s undisputed correspondence and in Acts, and it is precisely these contours that we see again in Eph. 3:1–13. If we turn first to Paul’s undisputed correspondence, we discover, as Best (1997a: 124–26) correctly argues, that Paul considered himself to be the apostle to the Gentiles par excellence (Rom. 1:5, 13; 11:13; 15:15–18; cf. 1 Cor. 15:8). In addition, he speaks of an agreement between himself and the “pillars” in Jerusalem that he was the apostle to the Gentiles and they, particularly Peter, were apostles to the Jews (Gal. 2:7–9).

We also find, however, that Paul had no quarrel with other Jewish Christians who preached the gospel among the Gentiles and who worked relatively independently of him. Cephas, for example, was certainly known to the predominantly Gentile Corinthian church, and he probably had traveled to Corinth to work among them. When Paul mentions Cephas in 1 Corinthians, however, he says nothing about Cephas’s violation of the Jerusalem agreement (1 Cor. 1:12; 3:22; 9:5; 15:5). Similarly, although Apollos arrived in Corinth independently of Paul and felt free to disagree with him on strategic details of the work there (1 Cor. 3:6–8; 16:12), Paul nevertheless viewed himself as united with Apollos in the common work of building up the Corinthian church (1 Cor. 3:8). Paul, then, certainly saw himself as the primary apostle to the Gentiles, but it also seems reasonable to think that he knew that others, independently of his own special role, understood and acted on the need to preach the gospel to the Gentiles.

This pattern emerges again in Acts. There, Peter takes the gospel to the Gentile Cornelius and his family in response to what could be called a revelation (Acts 10:1–11:18; cf. 15:7). After some initial hesitation, “the apostles and brothers who were in Judea” acknowledged the validity of the vision and accepted its implication that God had “also given to the Gentiles repentance for the purpose of life” (Acts 11:1–18; cf. 15:14). Despite this, and despite also having a role in proclaiming the gospel to Israel (Acts 9:15), Paul remains the primary means by which the gospel goes “far away to the Gentiles” (Acts 22:21; 26:17–18).

If we now turn back to Eph. 3:1–13, we discover the same pattern. Paul plays the chief strategic role in proclaiming the gospel to the Gentiles, a role that “was made known” to him “by revelation” (3:2–4, 6–13). This description nicely summarizes the picture in Acts and Galatians of how the insight concerning the Gentiles’ inclusion came to Paul (Acts 9:3–6, 15–16; 22:6–21; 26:12–18; Gal. 1:11–12). But the whole group of apostles and prophets also understood this insight (3:5). This too is an apt summary of the picture that emerges from Acts of a vision to Peter whose validity was subsequently recognized by others.

If we now put all this together, we can say that in 3:5 Paul contrasts the period prior to the revelation of the Gentiles’ full inclusion in God’s people, on equal terms with the Jews, with the period “now” (νῦν, nyn) in effect after that revelation. This revelation came not only to Paul at the time of his conversion but also to the other apostles and prophets in this new era, and it was revealed to them by the Spirit of God. Within this group, the apostles (including Paul) hold a special place, which Paul signals by calling them “holy.” He uses this unusual term for them because the link that most of them have with the historical Jesus gives them an especially critical role in the founding and guidance of the church.

[3:6] Paul next explains the content of the mystery that has “now been revealed.” It concerns the status of the Gentiles, and Paul describes this new status with three adjectives, each of which begins with a form of the preposition σύν (syn, together with).[38] A chart is perhaps the easiest way to convey the rhetorical effect of these compounded terms:



συγκληρονόμα (synklēronoma, heirs together with)

σύσσωμα (syssōma, one body together with)

συμμέτοχα τῆς ἐπαγγελίας (symmetocha tēs epangelias, sharers together with . . . in the promise)

It is clear, then, that the Gentiles are inheritors, one body, and sharers “together with” (σύν), but “together with” whom? The previous paragraph (2:19–22), with its own set of three σύν compounds, makes the answer clear. Gentile believers are now full participants in each of these three qualities with Jewish believers.[39]

The term συγκληρονόμος (synklēronomos) recalls the theme of inheritance that appears in several places in the letter’s opening prayer sections (1:11, 14, 18). It is an eschatological theme, looking forward to the time when God’s people will receive their inheritance (1:11, 14; 5:5; cf. 1:18; Col. 3:24). This, in turn, recalls the biblical theme that God had promised Abraham the inheritance of the land.[40] In Galatians and Romans Paul has described Jews and Gentiles who are united in their common faith in Christ as the people who will see the ultimate fulfillment of this biblical promise (Gal. 3:6–4:7; Rom. 4:1–25). Their inheritance would not be a geographical region at the eastern end of the Mediterranean Sea, but, as Paul makes especially clear in Romans, a glorious existence within a renewed creation as God’s adopted and beloved children (Rom. 4:13–14; 8:14–30; cf. Gal. 3:29; 4:4–6; 6:15).[41] Those ideas are also present, although in a more subtle form, in Ephesians (1:5, 13–14; 2:10, 15; 3:9; 4:13, 23–24).

If the concept of inheritance has such rich roots in the OT, how could Paul consider the coinheritance of Gentile and Jewish Christians to be a previously unknown mystery (3:5, 9)? The previously unknown element lies in the σύν. As we saw above (on 3:5), the OT and Jewish literature of the Second Temple period is replete with references to the inclusion of the Gentiles in the worship of God to come in the eschatological period of Israel’s restoration. The full equality of Gentiles with Jews in a newly constituted humanity, however, was not revealed previously.[42]

The second term, σύσσωμα, appears here for the first time in all known literature, and it is possible that Paul invented it.[43] Its two components are very common, however, and so the meaning of the term is not in doubt. It recalls Paul’s claim in 2:16 that Christ has reconciled both Jews and Gentiles to God “in one body” (ἐν ἑνὶ σώματι, en heni sōmati) through his death on the cross (cf. 4:4). It also recalls his description in 1:23 of the church as Christ’s “body” (σῶμα, sōma; cf. 4:12, 16; 5:23, 29–30). Gentile believers are, then, “one body together with” Jewish believers, and this new, composite group is the church.

The final term, συμμέτοχα, is also an unusual word, although not as rare as σύσσωμα (pace Ellicott 1859: 60). Origen was apparently unfamiliar with it and seems to have thought, based on its use in 5:7, that it had a negative connotation (Heine 2002: 217; cf. Josephus, J.W. 1.486). There is no sign of that here, however, where it seems simply to be a more intense form of the adjective μέτοχος (metochos, “sharing in, partner,” BDAG 643), chosen perhaps for rhetorical reasons, since it begins with a form of σύν, like the other two terms.

The Gentiles are sharers together with the Jews τῆς ἐπαγγελίας (tēs epangelias, in the promise).[44] What is this promise? Paul is probably thinking especially of the promise to Abraham that through him all the Gentiles would be blessed (Gal. 3:8; Rom. 4:13), a promise that in Gal. 3:14 seems to merge with the biblical promise of the eschatological outpouring of God’s Spirit (cf. Eph. 1:13; Isa. 32:15; 44:3; Ezek. 11:19; 36:26–27; 37:14; Joel 3:1–2; cf. Acts 1:4; 2:33).[45]

Paul next supplies two phrases that indicate how these three characteristics have come to his Gentile readers. They are full and equal participants with others in the newly constituted people of God because they too are ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ (en Christō Iēsou, in Christ Jesus). In 1:10, Paul has identified the mystery as God’s intention to sum up all things in heaven and on earth “in Christ” (cf. 3:10–11), and in 2:11–22 Paul has described how Christ has started to accomplish the earthly part of this plan by making Jewish and Gentile believers into one new human being “in” himself “through” his death on the cross (2:13, 15; cf. Gnilka 1971: 168–69). Not all Jews and Gentiles, therefore, are now one people, but only those who are “in Christ.” One becomes “in Christ,” and therefore part of the one, new multiethnic people of God διὰ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου (dia tou euangeliou, through the gospel; cf. 1 Cor. 4:15), that is, by hearing the gospel preached and believing it (1:13).

[3:7] Using language that is reminiscent of 3:2 (and of Col. 1:23, 25), Paul now returns to his own role in bringing the mystery he has just described out of hiding (3:2–4). He has become, he says, a διάκονος (diakonos, servant) of the gospel. Διάκονος means, in a general sense, one who assists another (e.g., Matt. 22:13; John 2:5, 9; BDAG 230), but Paul frequently uses this and the closely related words διακονέω (diakoneō, serve) and διακονία (diakonia, service) to refer to his special work of urging people to be reconciled to God through faith in Christ (1 Cor. 3:5; 2 Cor. 3:3, 6; 4:1; 5:18; 6:3–4; 11:23; 1 Tim. 1:12). In Romans he could speak of his “service” (διακονία) as synonymous with his role as “apostle of the Gentiles” (11:13), and that concept is close to the thought he develops here. Paul serves the gospel in the sense that he preaches it to the Gentiles, enabling them to hear and believe it (cf. 1:13) and in this way become incorporated into the new, multiethnic people of God (cf. 2:11–22; 3:6).[46]

Paul’s strategic role in the proclamation of the gospel to the Gentiles came to him “according to” (κατά, kata) a graciously given gift from God.[47] In 4:7 Paul will say similarly that each believer has been “given grace according to [κατά] the measure of the gift of Christ,” and then in 4:12 that these gifts are intended “for the building up of the body of Christ” (cf. 1 Pet. 4:10). Christ equips every believer with a gift for edifying the body, and Paul’s own gift was the foundational proclamation of the gospel to the Gentiles as one of the apostles and prophets (2:20; 3:2, 5; 4:11).

Paul was given this gift “according to [κατά] the effect [ἐνέργειαν, energeian] of his [God’s] power [δυνάμεως, dynameōs].”[48] Just as in 1:19 and 3:20, so here Paul seems to distinguish between the “effective power” (ἐνέργεια) and the “potential power” (δύναμις) of God.[49] God put his potential power into effect when he made Paul a servant of the gospel. Paul is thinking principally of his conversion from persecutor of the church to proclaimer of the gospel to the Gentiles, something that only God’s power could effect and that, whenever Paul mentions it, he couples with God’s grace, as he does here (Gal. 1:13–16; 2:8; cf. 1 Cor. 15:8–10; 1 Tim. 1:12–14). He may also be thinking, however, of the continuing effectiveness of God’s power in his ministry, despite his imprisonment (3:1; 4:1) and suffering (3:13; cf. Col. 1:29; see Bruce 1984: 317; O’Brien 1999: 239).

In 1:19 Paul has prayed that his readers might understand the vastness of the power that God has put into effect for them. Here in 3:7, he may be subtly presenting himself to them as a practical example of how this works. God’s great power was behind Paul’s own conversion from persecutor to herald of the good news and remains effective in his ministry despite his imprisonment (v. 1) and suffering (v. 13).

The repetition from 3:2 of the concepts of Paul’s particular role in proclaiming the gospel to the Gentiles (v. 2: οἰκονομία, oikonomia, task of administration; v. 7: διάκονος, diakonos, servant) and of God’s gracious gift to him of that role (v. 2: χάρις, charis, grace; δίδωμι, didōmi, give; v. 7: δωρεά, dōrea, gift; χάρις, charis, grace; δίδωμι, didōmi, give) form a rhetorically effective close to the long sentence that constitutes this section (vv. 1–7). As happens elsewhere in Paul’s Letters, however, the close of one section already announces the major concern of the section that follows it (on this feature of Romans, see Dahl 1977: 82–83). Here, Paul’s concern with his service to the gospel anticipates the next paragraph (3:8–13), where he describes the way he has carried out this service (Best 1998: 313).

Summary

After dwelling on the way God has used his great power to include Paul’s formerly hopeless Gentile readers into his people, Paul begins in 3:1–7 to pray that God might empower his readers to understand the vastness of Christ’s love (3:14, 18–19). Before he can complete this thought, however, Paul breaks off in midsentence to describe to his readers his own role in God’s plan to place Gentile believers on the same footing with Jewish believers in a newly constituted people. God has graciously given to Paul, along with other apostles and prophets, the insight that through Christ’s death God was making Gentile believers one body together with, heirs together with, and sharers together with Jewish believers. This complete equality between Gentiles and Jews in one new people of God is something that neither Paul nor the other apostles and prophets could have known apart from God’s revelation of it to them. It is in this sense a “mystery.”

God has given Paul the responsibility of administering this mystery to the Gentiles, of making known to them that they can have a place in God’s people if they believe the gospel. When God gave this responsibility to Paul, he was the least likely person God could have chosen for the task, but this is how God works: he uses his great power in gracious ways to transform his enemies into his servants.



Additional Notes

3:1. The way in which Paul refers to the relationship between his imprisonment and Christ varies widely among ancient witnesses to the letter’s text. In one strongly attested tradition, Paul says that he is the prisoner τοῦ Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ. This reading appears in some of the most ancient witnesses (e.g., 𝔓46, B, A, Origen, Coptic) and is geographically diverse, showing up in Alexandrian (e.g., 𝔓46, B, A) as well as most Byzantine, and some Western (e.g., two manuscripts of the Old Latin, Pelagius) witnesses. It may well be the correct reading (Metzger 1994: 534, with some hesitation; Hoehner 2002: 420n1; Sellin 2008: 248).

Another set of witnesses, however, omits the name Ἰησοῦ. These include the early Alexandrian א; the Western trio D, F, and G; and such Byzantine witnesses as 256 and 2127. In addition to this strong external attestation is the possibility that an original τοῦ Χριστοῦ was expanded to τοῦ Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ under the influence of Philem. 1 and 9 (Best 1998: 294). All five references to Paul as a prisoner in the Pauline corpus also refer in some way to Jesus. If we set aside Eph. 3:1, only the two references in Philem. 1 and 9 are identical, and this makes it all the more likely that the particular expression found in those two references would have influenced the text of Eph. 3:1. The other “prisoner” references seem to have had a smaller impact on the text, but they illustrate what probably happened with Philem. 1, 9 and Eph. 3:1. Τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ (C Ψ) may have been influenced by 2 Tim. 1:8, and the expressions ἐν Χριστῷ (365), and ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ (lectionaries 156, 170, and 617) may have been influenced by Eph. 4:1.

It seems best, therefore, to assume that at an early date the name Ἰησοῦ was added to the text under the influence of the two references in Philemon.

3:3. An impressive list of both Alexandrian (𝔓46, B) and Western (F, G, two Old Latin manuscripts, “Ambrosiaster”) witnesses omits the ὅτι at the beginning of the verse. If this tradition is followed, then 3:3 begins a new sentence. The omission looks suspiciously like an attempt to simplify the enormous sentence that stretches from 3:1 through 3:7, however, and this suspicion grows with the realization that these long sentences, although difficult, are part of the distinctive style of this letter (Best 1998: 299). In addition, the inclusion of ὅτι has strong external support (Hoehner 2002: 425n2). It is found in early (א, A, C) and geographically diverse witnesses (א, D, most Byzantine manuscripts, and the Armenian, Vulgate, Syriac, Bohairic Coptic, and Syriac versions). Both internal and external evidence point toward its inclusion.





VI. Paul’s Divinely Given Task and His Suffering for the Gentiles (3:1–13)

A. Paul’s Role in the Administration of the Mystery (3:1–7)

B. How Paul Fulfills His Task (3:8–13)


B. How Paul Fulfills His Task (3:8–13)

If the previous section (3:1–7) was primarily about the link between Paul’s administrative responsibility and the mystery of the Gentiles’ inclusion in the church, then this section is chiefly devoted to the ways in which he has carried out that role (Schnackenburg 1991: 129; Best 1998: 292; Hoehner 2002: 453) and why the role was necessary. He has fulfilled the role that God gave him in two ways. First, he has proclaimed the good news of the unsearchable riches of Christ to the Gentiles (v. 8b), and second, he has illumined everyone, whether Jew or Gentile, about the mystery that the Creator of the universe has now revealed (v. 9).

Why is it necessary for Paul to proclaim the gospel to the Gentiles and the mystery to everyone? He does this in order to assemble a unified church of Jews and Gentiles who will bear witness to the inimical powers of the universe that the Creator’s purposes are being fulfilled (v. 10). This fulfillment, planned before time began, is taking place in the Messiah (v. 11) because those who believe in him, whether Jews or Gentiles, have the kind of relationship with God that friends have with each other, a relationship characterized by candid speech and confident access (v. 12). Paul probably thinks of this speech and access as primarily evident in prayer.

At this point the thought of prayer may have prompted Paul to remember that he had been digressing from a prayer. That prayer started with a reference to his imprisonment for the Gentiles, and he will get back to it shortly (in v. 14), but before doing so, he concludes his digression with an exhortation to his readers. Because of all that he has said about his strategic role in God’s “plan” for the universe, he asks his readers not to be discouraged that he is suffering for them. That suffering, he tells them, means their glory: it has brought them the gospel and made them part of God’s glorious inheritance in the saints (v. 13).

Like 3:1–7, this section has the marks of spontaneity. It is composed of two sentences, one of them very long (eighty-two words), and the other, by the standards of Eph. 1–3, short (fourteen words). The second, short sentence is designed to get the discourse back on track by returning to the theme of Paul’s suffering for the Gentiles, which in 3:1 started the digression that now comes to an end.



Exegesis and Exposition

8aTo me, the least of all the saints, 8bthis grace was given: to proclaim to the Gentiles the good news about the untraceable wealth of Christ 9and to illumine ⌜everyone⌝ about the administrative plan of the mystery hidden from eternity in the God who created all things, 10in order that the beautifully complex wisdom of God might now be made known through the church to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places 11according to his purpose from before the ages, which he carried out in the Messiah, Jesus our Lord, 12in whom we have boldness and confident access through faith in him. 13Therefore I ask you not to be discouraged in my sufferings for you, inasmuch as they are ⌜your⌝ glory.

[3:8a] Paul begins a new sentence, signaling the beginning of a new section. Just as he did at the beginning (v. 2) and end (v. 7) of the last sentence, he emphasizes his special responsibility (οἱκονομία, oikonomia, v. 2) in God’s purposes and describes that responsibility as the “grace” God has “given” him. As with 3:7, Paul’s conversion lies in the background. His reference to himself (ἐμοί, emoi, to me; cf. μοι, moi, vv. 2, 7) as ἐλαχιστοτέρῳ πάντων ἁγίων (elachistoterō pantōn hagiōn, least of all the saints) recalls the language of 1 Cor. 15:8–10. There Paul follows a description of the appearance of the resurrected Christ to him “last of all” with the comment that he is “the least [ἐλάχιστος, elachistos] of the apostles” because he “persecuted the church of God” (15:9). The dramatic change this appearance of Christ brought to him, he continues, was a result of God’s grace, a grace powerful enough to fuel his intense labor in the service of the gospel to the present day (15:10). In Ephesians, Paul speaks similarly of how his position as “the least of all the saints” contrasts sharply with the critical importance of his God-given role as proclaimer of the gospel and with the effective power that God has given to him to carry out this role (v. 7).

How can Paul expect readers, many of whom he does not personally know (3:2; 4:21), to appreciate this subtle reference to his conversion? The story of Paul’s conversion from persecutor of the church to preacher of the gospel was widely known during his lifetime, even among Christians he had never seen (Gal. 1:23), and it was the subject of praise to God (Gal. 1:24). It is not surprising, then, that he can assume his readers have heard this story.

The brief reference here to Paul as “the least of all the saints” has often played a role in discussion of the letter’s authorship. Defenders of Pauline authorship occasionally comment that a pseudonymous admirer of Paul would not have spoken in such an unflattering way of the apostle. To them, the statement is a sign of the letter’s authenticity.[1] It is not clear, however, that calling the pre-conversion Paul “the least of all the saints” would have been considered unflattering among ancient admirers. Luke was such an admirer but still gives a vivid impression of Paul’s murderous preconversion past in the buildup to his conversion (cf. Barn. 5.9).

Those who read the letter as a pseudonymous document often point out that the description of Paul’s conversion in Eph. 3:8 has been intensified in a way that is characteristic of the subapostolic age (Baur 2003: 2.33; Gnilka 1971: 170; Lincoln 1990: 183; cf. MacDonald 2000: 271). Two intensifications are thought to be especially revealing. First, the author of Ephesians seems to have transformed the simple ἐλάχιστος (elachistos, least) into the elaborate, and rather odd, ἐλαχιστότερος (elachistoteros), which is technically a comparative form of a superlative adjective and may mean “very least” (e.g., Lincoln 1990: 183; Schnackenburg 1991: 136; cf. MacDonald 2000: 264). Second, they point to an increasingly exaggerated portrait of Paul as a sinner. He begins in 1 Cor. 15:9 as merely the least of the apostles, but then becomes in Eph. 3:8 the least of all the saints, and in 1 Tim. 1:15 the first of sinners (e.g., Gnilka 1971: 170; Lincoln 1990: 183; Schnackenburg 1991: 136). This, they believe, falls in step with a tendency after Paul’s death to intensify the wickedness of the apostles in order to create a more impressive foil for the greatness of God’s grace.[2] Barnabas 5.9 seems to support the point: “And when he selected his own apostles who were about to preach his gospel, they were altogether lawless beyond all sin [ὄντας ὑπὲρ πᾶσαν ἁμαρτίαν ἀνομωτέρους, ontas hyper pasan hamartian anomōterous]. This was to show that he did not come to call the upright but sinners” (trans. Ehrman 2003).

Both “intensifications,” however, are far less than certain. The term ἐλαχιστότερος is extremely rare, but it is not “a kind of tour de force” (MHT 2:166), nor is it “a unique formation” (Abbott 1987: 85). Its first two occurrences in extant Greek literature are apparently here and in the mechanical writer Heron, who flourished in Alexandria during the mid 60s AD.[3] This is precisely the time that Ephesians was written, if Paul was the author.[4] Heron uses the word in quite pedestrian prose, as if it is nothing unusual, and it is not clear that it means anything other than “least.” It appears in a description of the different technical terms for the measurement of length: “Now least of all (πάντων δὲ ἐλαχιστότερον, pantōn de elachistoteron),” he says, “is the ‘finger’” (Heron, Def. 130.1.5). “Least of all” rather than “very least of all” seems to be a good translation here because Heron promptly divides the “finger” into the still-smaller components of one-half, one-third, and so on.

The idea that Paul’s wickedness became increasingly exaggerated with the march of time is even shakier. Although Barn. 5.9 may show a general tendency in this direction, it does not mention Paul and, as Wallace (1996: 302n26) points out, “is not autobiographical.” It is more likely that hyperbole about one’s position relative to other Christians or about past sins arose on occasion among those who believed God had been especially gracious to them. It is not only the genuine Paul of 1 Cor. 15:9 who uses this kind of language but also the genuine Ignatius: “Remember in your prayers the church in Syria,” he says to the Trallians, “of which I am not worthy to be considered a member, being as I am the very least [ἔσχατος, eschatos, literally, ‘last’] of them” (Trall. 13.1, trans. Holmes 2007; cf. Ign. Eph. 21.1). This could be another emergence of the tradition that started with 1 Cor. 15:9 and continued in Eph. 3:8 and 1 Tim. 1:15, but that seems unlikely since there is so little verbal agreement between Ignatius’s statement and the supposed tradition.[5] The lack of verbal agreement must count as evidence that there is no connection at all and that Christians, independently of one another, sometimes simply spoke this way.[6]

In light of the ambiguity of the evidence, then, it seems best to excuse Eph. 3:8a from the debate over the epistle’s authorship (cf. Aletti 2001: 185). A pseudonymous author could have written it, but nothing about the substance of the description is either uncharacteristic of Paul or especially characteristic of a later era.

Assuming on other grounds, then, that Paul is the letter’s author, it is probable that his experience of God’s grace in moving him from persecutor of the church to servant of the gospel, has led him to speak of himself in this way. His strategic role in God’s purposes (3:2), his insight into the union of Jewish and Gentile believers in one body (3:3–6), his proclamation of the gospel to the Gentiles (3:7–8), and his illumination of everyone about God’s plan (3:9)—these were due not to his own ability but to the graciousness of God and “the effect of his power” (3:7). Paul can therefore call the role that God has given him to proclaim the gospel to the Gentiles ἡ χάρις αὕτη (hē charis hautē, this grace; cf. 3:2; Gal. 2:7–9; 1 Cor. 3:10; Phil. 1:7; Rom. 1:5; 12:3; 15:15–16).

[3:8b–9] Αὕτη (hautē, this) points forward to two infinitives that describe the “grace” God has given to Paul in further detail. First, God has commissioned Paul τοῖς ἔθνεσιν εὐαγγελίσασθαι (tois ethnesin euangelisasthai, to proclaim to the Gentiles the good news [about . . .]). Paul last used the verb εὐαγγελίζω (euangelizō, proclaim the good news) in 2:17 to refer to Christ’s proclamation of peace with God to both “the far” (the Gentiles) and “the near” (the Jews). He has also just used the noun form of this verb, εὐαγγελίζω (euangelion, good news), in 3:6–7 to describe the gospel as the instrument through which Gentile and Jewish believers are united in one people. His role, then, is to be the means through which Christ proclaims to the Gentiles the good news of reconciliation with God (cf. Gal. 1:16; 2:7; Rom. 1:5; 15:15–16; 1 Tim. 2:7; Acts 9:15).

Rather than using the language of reconciliation to describe the content of the gospel, however, here Paul describes it as τὸ ἀνεξιχνίαστον πλοῦτος τοῦ Χριστοῦ (to anexichniaston ploutos tou Christou, the untraceable wealth of Christ). Paul has already used the term πλοῦτος (ploutos, wealth) three times in the letter to speak of the lavish nature of God’s relationship to his people:



In 1:7 God’s people receive “the wealth [τὸ πλοῦτος, to ploutos] of his grace” when he redeems them through Christ’s blood.

In 1:18 God’s people are to him an inheritance of great “wealth [ὁ πλοῦτος, ho ploutos]” (1:18; cf. 3:16).

In 2:7 God has given life to, raised, and seated his people together with Christ so that he might show to them “the surpassing wealth [τὸ . . . πλοῦτος] of his grace” for all time (2:7).

In 1:7 and 2:7, the wealth is the richness of God’s grace as it is visible in the death, resurrection, and exaltation of Christ. Here in 3:8b, then, the genitive expression τοῦ Χριστοῦ means not that the untraceable wealth is Christ himself (Lincoln 1990: 183–84; MacDonald 2000: 265), but that it is the grace of God shown in Christ (Pokorný 1992: 144–45; Hübner 1997: 188). The term ἀνεξιχνίαστος (anexichniastos, untraceable) is particularly appropriate for describing God’s grace in Christ here since Paul has just explained that God’s plan to include Gentiles and Jews on equal terms among his people “in Christ Jesus” would be utterly unknown apart from the special revelation of it to Paul, the apostles, and the prophets (3:3, 5–6).[7] No one would have been able to “trace out” the logic of the Scriptures to this conclusion; God had to reveal it.

The thought in 3:8b is similar to that of Rom. 9–11, where God surprisingly shows the “wealth” (ὁ πλοῦτος) of his glory to the Gentiles (9:23) so that they experience the “wealth” (πλοῦτος) of his mercy (11:12), but does this in a way that, also surprisingly, will include formerly unbelieving Jews (11:25–32). Paul calls the unexpected inclusion of “all Israel” within God’s people in the future a “mystery” (μυστήριον, mystērion; 11:25), and he praises the whole unpredictable and merciful arrangement as “the depth of the wealth [πλούτου] of the wisdom and knowledge of God,” whose ways are “untraceable” (ἀνεξιχνίαστοι; 11:33).

Second, God has commissioned Paul φωτίσαι πάντας (phōtisai pantas, to illumine everyone). The term πάντας (pantas, everyone) is masculine, and so it does not refer back to the neuter term ἔθνεσιν (ethnesin, Gentiles) in 3:8.﻿[8] Here, then, Paul is called to explain not only to Gentiles but also to everyone, whether Jew or Gentile, “the plan of the mystery” revealed to him about the full partnership of Gentile believers with Jewish believers (3:6). As Paul says in his Letter to the Romans, he is obligated to proclaim the gospel to Greek, barbarian, wise, foolish, Jew, or Gentile (Rom. 1:14, 16; Hoehner 2002: 455). As Romans demonstrates, this was not always an evangelistic task in the sense of calling unbelievers to faith. Paul sometimes felt that it was his apostolic responsibility to preach the gospel to believers in such a way that he clearly showed its implications for ethnic unity (Rom. 11:13; 12:3; 14:1–15:13).

Once again (cf. v. 5), Paul emphasizes that the mystery of the unity of Gentile with Jewish believers was unknown until God revealed it in the gospel. He describes the mystery in three ways.

First, he says, it was ἀποκεκρυμμένος (apokekrymmenos, hidden). The perfect tense of this adjectival participle emphasizes the mystery’s hiddenness: God’s plan to place Jews and Gentiles on an equal footing within his newly constituted people was known only to God prior to his revelation of it to Paul and other apostles and prophets (vv. 2–5, 7–8).[9] It was, as Paul has just said, “untraceable.”

Second, the mystery was hidden ἀπὸ τῶν αἰώνων (apo tōn aiōnōn). This means either that it was hidden “from the Aeons”—the evil spiritual forces that Paul refers to elsewhere in the letter (1:21; 2:2–3; 6:12), including the next clause (v. 10)—or that it was hidden “from ages past.”[10] The term αἰών (aiōn, age) was beginning to take on connotations of a personal cosmic power in the first century (see the additional note on 2:2), but when Paul uses this term elsewhere to speak of the hiddenness of God’s “wisdom” or of “the mystery,” it clearly describes the massive length of time that these remained hidden (1 Cor. 2:7; Col. 1:26; cf. Rom. 16:25). Any other connotation here is unlikely.

Third, the mystery was hidden “in the God who created [κτίσαντι, ktisanti] all things.” This phrase continues two important themes of the letter so far: God chose a people for himself prior to the world’s creation (1:9–10; cf. 1:4–5, 11; 2:10), and this people is itself a new humanity or a new creation (2:10, 15; 4:13; 5:31–32). Prior to the time that his Spirit revealed it to Paul (and other apostles and prophets), only God knew that in Christ he would fully overcome the division between Jews and Gentiles.[11] God has graciously given Paul a strategic administrative role (οἰκονομία, oikonomia, v. 2) in the plan (οἰκονομία; v. 9) according to which this mystery is being worked out: he is to preach the gospel to the Gentiles (v. 8) and to enlighten everyone—whether Gentile or Jew—about the ethnically inclusive nature of this new creation.

[3:10] Paul next introduces a purpose clause (ἵνα, hina, in order that) that grammatically could give either the reason why the mystery was hidden (Abbott 1897: 88; Haupt 1902a: 105–6; Muddiman 2001: 160) or the reason why Paul preached the gospel to the Gentiles and enlightened everyone (Alford 1857: 103).[12] This second option is far more likely to be correct. The purpose is that something “might be made known” (γνωρισθῇ, gnōristhē), and since this thought is consistent with Paul’s preaching (εὐαγγελίσασθαι, euangelisasthai; v. 8) and enlightening (φωτίσαι, phōtisai; v. 9), Paul is now explaining why he preaches the untraceable riches of Christ to the Gentiles and enlightens everyone about God’s previously hidden plan to unite Jews and Gentiles in one body (Eadie 1883: 230). He does this to make something known.

This something is “the πολυποίκιλος [polypoikilos, beautifully complex] wisdom of God.” This rare term combines the more common adjective ποικίλος (poikilos), meaning “many-coloured, spotted, pied, dappled, wrought in various colours, changeful, diversified, manifold” (LSJ 1430), with the common adverb πολύς (polys), meaning “many.” Πολυποίκιλος connoted complex variety (Sib. Or. 1.89; 12.149), sometimes in crafted items such as a multicolored veil (Euripides, Iph. taur. 1150) or a floral wreath of many different flowers (Eubulus [Comic], Fragmenta 3.1–4.2; Athenaeus, Deipn. 15.24.32; cf. Sib. Or. 1.291). It could also be used of complex emotions (Sib. Or. 8.120) and reasoning processes (Herodorus, Fragmenta 24b.7–8). Here in Eph. 3:10 it seems to refer to the many complex facets of God’s wisdom. Just as the wealth of Christ is “untraceable” (ἀνεξιχνίαστον, anexichniaston), according to 3:8, so now Paul describes the wisdom of God as “very many-sided” (BDAG 847).[13]

Perhaps there is also a hint of the unfathomable wisdom of God in the creation of the world. This theme was common in antiquity, appearing in Greek philosophy (Critias, DK 88B25.12),[14] the Jewish and Christian Scriptures (Prov. 8:22–31; Job 28:20–27), and in other Jewish literature from the Second Temple period (Sir. 42:15–25; 43:1–33; Bar. 3:29–37; Wis. 8:1; 1QHa 9.7–8, 13–14, 19–20).[15] A reference to God’s wisdom in creation would not be out of place here, on the heels of Paul’s description of God as the one who “created all things” (v. 9). The translation “beautifully complex,” then, might be even more appropriate than “very many-sided.”

Paul probably thinks of “the beautifully complex wisdom of God” as especially evident in the unity of Jewish and Gentile believers in the church (v. 6). This is the mystery that was utterly inaccessible to human understanding until God, in whom it was hidden, revealed it to the apostles and prophets, and especially to Paul (vv. 2, 5, 7–9). The full unity of Jewish with Gentile believers in the one body of Christ, moreover, is the “creation” of a “new human being” (2:15–16).[16] All this is evidence of the vast complexity of God’s wisdom, a wisdom now evident not merely in the beautiful diversity of his creation but also in the surprising way he is restoring this creation after the ravages of sin.

Αἱ ἀρχαὶ καὶ αἱ ἐξουσίαι (hai archai kai hai exousiai, the rulers and authorities) have played a role in leading all humanity into transgression, sin, and death. According to a Jewish tradition that was influential during Paul’s era, Gen. 6:1–6 describes how such beings had strayed from the place in heaven that God had assigned to them at creation and had introduced humanity to various forms of wickedness, including the magical arts (e.g., CD-A 2.17–21; 4QEnocha 3–4QEnochc 6; 1 En. 6–16; T. Naph. 3.4–5). Some form of that tradition lies behind 1 Pet. 3:19–20; Jude 6; and 2 Pet. 2:4–5 and may also lie in the background here (cf. Schwindt 2002: 367–69). In light of the way Paul speaks of “the rulers and authorities” elsewhere in the letter, there can, in any case, be little doubt that Paul considered these figures to be thoroughly evil spiritual beings who exercised power over the unbelieving world (2:1–2; 6:12).[17] The church is unified across ethnic lines and is a newly created human being. By its very existence as a unified body, then, the church makes known to the evil spiritual rulers and authorities the vastness of God’s creative wisdom: he not only created the universe with its endless variety, but in a wholly surprising way he has also begun to restore the crowning achievement of his creation—humanity—to its original unity.

The rulers and authorities to whom the ethnically unified church makes all this known occupy the same “heavenly” (ἐπουράνιος, epouranios) world that God (1:3, 20), Christ Jesus (1:20; 2:6), and even believers (2:6; cf. 1:20–23) and their blessings (1:3) occupy (cf. 2:2; 6:12; and the comments on 2:2). The powers, however, are conquered and beneath the Messiah’s feet (1:20–22). Since the church is one with the risen and enthroned Christ (2:6), the powers are also conquered and beneath the church’s feet (cf. 1:20–23). From this position with Christ, the church can “now” (νῦν, nyn) testify to the powers that, despite their ability even in the present to work in “the sons of disobedience” (2:2), to make strategic plans to trouble God’s people (6:11), and to shoot their “ignited missiles” at them (6:16), their designs will ultimately fail.

It is likely that for Christians in Roman Asia in the first century, the earthly rulers and authorities—the deified and reigning emperors who were worshiped in the imperial cult and who, through governors and magistrates and loyal citizens, often made life difficult for believers—would have provided evidence of the continuing potency of the evil heavenly powers.[18] If so, then Paul’s claim that the church provides counterevidence of God’s superior power would come as a welcome encouragement to his readers.

[3:11] The vast and complex wisdom of God was made known to the evil spiritual rulers and authorities κατὰ πρόθεσιν τῶν αἰώνων (kata prothesin tōn aiōnōn, according to his purpose from before the ages). Paul now reaches back to a prominent theme in the letter’s opening benedictory prayer—that everything involved in the redemption of his people and the reuniting of creation in Christ, including the revelation of the mystery, happened according to a conscious decision of God prior to the beginning of time (1:5, 9, 11). Here in 3:11 he adds that the revelation of God’s beautifully complex wisdom to the evil powers through the church was also in God’s plan from the beginning.

The Greek is a little unusual: the expression τῶν αἰώνων has the article and is plural, and so a natural translation would be “according to the predetermination of the Aeons.” A few interpreters (most notably Schlier 1957: 157) have opted for this reading, taking τῶν αἰώνων as an objective genitive and trying to explain the text as a reference to God’s predetermination of personal, cosmic powers. Not only does the use of τῶν αἰώνων in 3:21 in a strictly chronological sense make this reading unlikely, however, but τῶν αἰώνων makes much better contextual sense if it is a “genitive of quality” or an “attributive genitive” (BDF §165; Wallace 1996: 86–88). A reference to God’s “purpose from before the ages” fits neatly with the predestinarian echoes of the benedictory prayer that are already reverberating in Paul’s use of the phrase κατὰ πρόθεσιν (kata prothesin, according to the purpose; cf. 1:9, 11). The prefix προ- (pro-, before) attached to πρόθεσιν, moreover, probably has a chronological element that governs the genitive phrase τῶν αἰώνων and gives the whole phrase a strong resemblance to 1 Cor. 2:7 (ἣν [σοφίαν] προώρισεν ὁ θεὸς πρὸ τῶν αἰώνων, hēn [sophian] proōrisen ho theos pro tōn aiōnōn, which [wisdom] God predestined before the ages; Sellin 1992: 98–99).

This eternal purpose God ἐποίησεν (epoiēsen) in Christ. Does this mean that God “made” the plan in Christ before time began (e.g., Calvin 1965: 164; Robinson 1904: 171–72; Best 1998: 328), or does it mean that when the right time came, God “carried out” his age-old plan in Christ (e.g., Lincoln 1990: 189; Pokorný 1992: 147; O’Brien 1999: 248–49; Hoehner 2002: 463–64)? The verb ποιέω (poieō, make, do) can mean either “make” or “carry out,” but here Paul probably speaks of God carrying out his purpose in Christ. Although this is the less-usual meaning of the term, Paul can use it this way elsewhere in Ephesians (2:3), and his only other use of πρόθεσις in the letter links it to God working (ἐνεργέω, energeō) all things (1:11; Lincoln 1990: 189).

This understanding makes good sense of the unusually elaborate reference to Christ that follows ἐποίησεν: ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ κυρίῳ ἡμῶν (en tō Christō Iēsou tō kyriō hēmōn, in the Messiah, Jesus our Lord). Elsewhere in Ephesians when Paul uses the names Christ, Jesus, and Lord in combination with each other and the pronoun “our” (1:3, 17; 5:20; 6:24), he always uses the order “our Lord Jesus Christ” (ὁ κύριος ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦς Χριστός).
