Here, however, he places the title “Christ” first and uses the article with it as if he wanted to emphasize that “Jesus our Lord” is “the Messiah” (cf. Col. 2:6). God decided before the world began not only to fulfill his purposes for the universe through his anointed king Jesus but also to make the fulfillment of his purposes through Messiah Jesus known to the inimical spiritual powers of the universe.

[3:12] Prior to 3:11, Paul’s last use of the first-person plural was in 2:11–18, where he said that “the blood of Christ” (2:13), shed on the cross (2:16), brought unity to Jews and Gentiles. “Through him,” he said in 2:18, “we both have access [προσαγωγή, prosagōgē] in one Spirit to the Father.” Paul now recalls this language, using both the first-person plural and the term προσαγωγή again. Here, however, his point is that the access Jewish and Gentile believers have together to God in Christ stands as a witness to the evil powers concerning God’s unsearchable, complex wisdom.

Perhaps the memory that, at this point in his dictation of the letter, he is digressing from an intercessory prayer prompts Paul to nuance the notion of believers’ access to God so that it refers specifically to access in prayer. Believers do not simply have access but ἡ παρρησία καὶ προσαγωγὴ ἐν πεποιθήσει (hē parrēsia kai prosagōgē en pepoithēsei, boldness and confident access). The term παρρησία (parrēsia, boldness) appears to have been used first in political contexts to refer to the freedom of speech granted to citizens of Athens in the public assembly (e.g., Euripides, Hipp. 420–23).[19] By Paul’s time it had acquired both philosophical and moral connotations, particularly where telling others the truth about life in a philosophical discourse or speaking frankly in friendship were the issues (e.g., Aristotle, Eth. Nic. 9.2.9 [9.1165a.29–30]; Let. Aris. 125). Although people certainly could speak with inappropriate harshness (and Cynic philosophers were often charged with this fault), a sensitive candor in one’s relationship with others was a sign of true friendship (e.g., Plutarch, Adul. amic.). This made παρρησία an appropriate term to use in Hellenistic Jewish and Christian literature for prayer (Job 22:26 LXX; 1 John 5:14–15; Philo, Heir 14; Josephus, Ant. 5.38).

Paul can use both the verb παρρησιάζομαι (parrēsiazomai, speak freely) and the noun παρρησία for the frank speech that those “in Christ” can have with each other (Philem. 1:8; cf. 2 Cor. 7:4) or for the bold proclamation of the gospel (1 Thess. 2:2; Phil. 1:20; Eph. 6:19–20; cf. 2 Cor. 3:12). The source of this “freedom” (ἐλευθερία, eleutheria) of speech (2 Cor. 3:17) is the intimate and open relationship that the believer has with Christ (2 Cor. 3:4–18). Here the thought is similar to 2 Cor. 3:4–18. Because they are in Christ (ἐν ᾧ, en hō, in whom), both Jewish and Gentile believers have access to God and may speak freely with him.

This access is also characterized by πεποίθησις (pepoithēsis), a term that appears only here and in the undisputed Pauline letters, where it means “confidence” (BDAG 796). Paul sometimes uses it to speak of confidence in other people (2 Cor. 1:15; 8:22), sometimes of confidence “in the flesh” (Phil. 3:3–4), and sometimes, when God, through Christ, is the source of one’s strength, of confidence in one’s competence to fulfill the task God has given (2 Cor. 3:4–5). Here in Eph. 3:12, in a way that is reminiscent of 2 Cor. 3:4–5, it is only ἐν ᾧ (en hō, in him [Christ]) that believers have προσαγωγὴ ἐν πεποιθήσει (prosagōgē en pepoithēsei, confident access) to God.

Because they are “in Christ,” then, both Jewish and Gentile believers have a relationship with God so close that they can speak freely with him. This access is also characterized by confidence that he will hear and welcome what they have to say.

Believers appropriate this freedom of speech and confident access to God διὰ τῆς πίστεως αὐτοῦ (dia tēs pisteōs autou). This could mean “through his [i.e., Christ’s] faith” and refer to Christ’s faithfulness to God, especially in his obedient death on the cross; O’Brien (1999: 249) has provided a reasonable case for this meaning. The notion of trusting Christ, he says, has already been supplied by the phrase ἐν πεποιθήσει (en pepoithēsei, in confidence), and in 2:18 Christ is the means (δι᾿ αὐτοῦ, di’ autou, through him) by which access (προσαγωγή) to God is obtained.[20] Redundancy in Ephesians, however, should come as no surprise. Moreover, in 3:17 Paul speaks of Christ dwelling in the hearts of his readers διὰ τῆς πίστεως (dia tēs pisteōs, through faith), and this can refer only to his readers’ faith.[21] The similar expression here, then, is also probably a reference to “faith in Christ.”

[3:13] Paul brings his lengthy digression to a close by circling back to the theme of his suffering, the theme that, in a manner reminiscent of 2 Cor. 2:14, sparked the lengthy reflection on his own place in God’s administration of his plan to unite all things in Christ (vv. 2–12). Just as 3:1 spoke of his imprisonment “for” (ὑπέρ, hyper) his Gentile readers, so here too he speaks of his sufferings “for” (ὑπέρ) them.

He begins with a conjunction (διό, dio, therefore) that draws an inference either from the immediately preceding statement (“in whom we have boldness and confident access through faith in him”; v. 12) or from the entire preceding section. Since the conjunction introduces a clause that brings the reader back to the theme of 3:1, Paul probably refers back to the entire digression. All that he has said in 3:2–12 leads to this point.

Precisely here, however, Paul’s Greek becomes ambiguous. In the phrase αἰτοῦμαι μὴ ἐγκακεῖν (aitoumai mē enkakein), the term αἰτοῦμαι (aitoumai) could mean either to ask in prayer or simply to ask someone to do something. Since no subject is expressed, moreover, Paul could be referring either to his own discouragement or to that of his readers. Ancient commentators fluent in Paul’s native tongue could take the phrase either way. Theodoret thought Paul was asking God to help him “bear nobly the troubles befalling me” (Theodoret [R. Hill 2001: 2.44]). Theophylact thought he was asking his readers not to be troubled and discouraged (PG 124:1073).[22]

How do we sort this out? First, although the theme of prayer is in the air (3:1, 12, 14), Paul is not yet ready to return to his own prayer for his readers. That will not happen until 3:14, where the repetition of τούτου χάριν (toutou charin, on account of this) clearly demarcates Paul’s return to prayer from what has gone before. From a lexical standpoint, moreover, there is no reason to translate αἰτοῦμαι as “I pray” rather than “I ask” (Robinson 1904: 173; cf. Best 1998: 331). Second, it is true that “suffering” (θλῖψις, thlipsis) sometimes led to emotional turmoil for Paul (2 Cor. 1:8–9; 7:5–6; cf. Phil. 2:27), but to strike that note here would be odd. Nothing in 3:2–12 prepares the reader for a reference to the inner suffering that Paul’s often-difficult ministry involved. Instead, Paul celebrates God’s gift to him of his role in proclaiming the gospel to the Gentiles (3:2, 7–8).

Paul, then, is asking his readers not to “be discouraged” (ἐγκακέω, enkakeō) by his sufferings. The term ἐγκακέω could refer to a failure to perform one’s duty (Polybius, Hist. 4.19.10), but in the NT it always means “grow weary” (Gal. 6:9; 2 Thess. 3:13) or “be discouraged” (2 Cor. 4:1, 16; Luke 18:1). In 2 Cor. 4:16 it refers to an inner disposition: the suffering of Paul and his coworkers (4:7–12) has not “discouraged” (ἐγκακέω) them, he says, but rather their “inner person” (ὁ ἔσω, ho esō) is being renewed day by day (Robinson 1904: 173). Here in Eph. 3:13 Paul also refers to an inner disposition of his readers, as demonstrated a few phrases later by his prayer that they would be strengthened “in the inner human being” (εἰς τὸν ἔσω ἄνθρωπον, eis ton esō anthrōpon; 3:16).

Since 3:1 spoke specifically of his imprisonment, the hardships Paul has encountered in prison form the specific reason for his readers’ discouragement (cf. Phil. 1:17; 4:14). If Paul wrote this letter during the imprisonment described in Acts 28, then by the end of that period he had been a prisoner about five years (Acts 24:27; 27:9; 28:11; 28:16, 30). Although many of Paul’s readers knew him only by reputation (see 3:2 and the comments on that verse), they may well have been discouraged that “the apostle to the Gentiles” had for a number of years been unable to travel freely and proclaim the gospel in the manner described in 3:2–12 (cf. Cassidy 2001: 96–97).

If they were being marginalized in their own cities and neighborhoods, then Paul’s fate may have seemed like a reflection of their own difficulties. During this period more than a few Christians in Ephesus must have wondered from time to time whether their commitment to the God of the gospel was a mistake. With their refusal to participate in the imperial cult or to sacrifice to the local deities, had they only succeeded in angering the gods who had placed Rome in power? Were Paul’s troubles—and their own—a result of Christianity’s demand for exclusive loyalty to the God of the Jews and his Messiah? A large part of the purpose of Ephesians may well be to urge such discouraged Christians to remember who the God they worship is and what he is doing through his Messiah and the Messiah’s people, the church. They worship the Creator of the universe who is now, through Christ and the church, putting the universe back together after the ravages of sin.

Here, however, in a way that is consistent with 3:2–12, Paul concentrates on his own role, and specifically on the role of his “sufferings” (θλίψεις, thlipseis) in this grand design. His sufferings are “for” (ὑπέρ, hyper) them, and they should not be discouraged “inasmuch as” (ἥτις, hētis) his sufferings are their “glory” (δόξα, doxa).[23] When Paul speaks of suffering for others in other contexts, he has in mind the trouble, both physical and emotional, that he has endured in the course of his faithfulness to his commission to preach the gospel among the Gentiles. This faithfulness in the midst of suffering has brought life to those who have believed his proclamation (2 Cor. 4:7–12; cf. 1 Thess. 2:2, 9; 2 Cor. 2:14–16; Phil. 1:12–13; Col. 1:24). By the time Paul wrote Ephesians, many in his audience would have had no personal contact with him, but Paul considered himself an apostle to all Gentile Christians, even those whom he had never met (Rom. 1:11–15; 11:13; 15:14–16). Despite his physical and personal distance from his readers, his suffering was for them. Paul’s comment here, then, is close in meaning to Col. 1:24, where he refers to his sufferings on behalf of his readers in Colossae as suffering for the whole body of Christ, which is the church, and as a participation in the suffering of Christ himself.

What does Paul mean when he tells the Ephesians that his “sufferings” are their δόξα (doxa, glory)? Most commentators understand the term in a noneschatological sense as simply the “honor” or “dignity” that belongs to Paul’s readers as a result of the way God brought the gospel to them. They have “glory” because God has provided them with good things at the expense of his own Son and the affliction of his servants (e.g., Chrysostom, Hom. Eph., hom. 7; NPNF 13:81; Alford 1857: 104; Ellicott 1859: 66; cf. Eadie 1883: 239; Hoehner 2002: 470), or because they can rejoice in how God powerfully used Paul for their conversion despite his many troubles (Calvin 1965: 165; 1973: 271; Muddiman 2001: 164).

Despite the wide support that this reading of the term has received over the centuries, the connection between δόξα and suffering elsewhere in the Pauline corpus makes it unlikely. Elsewhere in Ephesians, δόξα is usually something that belongs to God (1:12, 14, 17; 3:16, 21) or to his grace (1:6), but a reasonable argument can be made that in 1:18 “the saints” are God’s inheritance and that they possess a richness of δόξα (cf. Col. 1:27; see the comments on 1:18 above). Since this description comes directly after Paul’s prayer that his readers might understand the “hope” of their calling, the term δόξα in Eph. 1:18 probably carries an eschatological nuance (cf. Col. 3:4). Here too, then, Paul’s suffering for his readers is their glory because his faithful proclamation of the gospel, in spite of the suffering that this faithfulness entails, has led to their salvation (1:13) and to a partial experience of the “glory” that one day will be theirs in full.

This thought is only a slight variation on the theme in Paul’s earlier letters that the suffering of Christians, and of Christian apostles in particular, will eventually give way to glory for those who suffer (2 Cor. 4:16–17; Rom. 8:18; cf. Phil. 3:21). It is a variation because here in Ephesians the one who suffers is not the one who is glorified. Instead, his suffering leads to the glorification of others. This development reappears, fully articulated, in Paul’s last letter: “Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, from the seed of David, according to my gospel, for which I suffer to the point of imprisonment as a criminal. But the word of God is not imprisoned. Because of this I endure everything for the elect, that they might experience salvation in Christ Jesus with eternal glory [δόξα]” (2 Tim. 2:8–10).[24]

Summary

In 3:8–13 Paul continues his digression on the role that God has graciously given him in his plan to unify Gentile and Jewish believers into one people who belong to God. Here Paul’s focus turns to how he fulfilled this role, its ultimate purpose, and the encouragement his readers should take from these elements of his role. Paul has fulfilled his responsbility by proclaiming the gospel to the Gentiles and by proclaiming to everyone, whether Jew or Gentile, the nature of God’s plan to unify both ethnic groups into one newly created humanity. The plan’s purpose was ultimately the proclamation to God’s cosmic enemies of the beautifully complex nature of God’s wisdom: through the death of Christ, God has killed the enmity between Jews and Gentiles and formed a people, united across ethnic lines, in whom his presence lives. Paul tells his Gentile readers not to be discouraged, because he is suffering in the process of fulfilling his part in this grand plan, for his suffering means their glorification.



Additional Notes

3:9. In some early witnesses (א, A, 424c, 6, 1739, 1881, Origen, Hilary, Jerome, Ambrosiaster) πάντας is missing. Without this term, the text would say that Paul was assigned φωτίσαι τίς ἡ οἰκονομία τοῦ μυστηρίου (to bring to light what the plan of the mystery . . . is), and the recipients of this illumination would remain unexpressed. It might seem, then, that πάντας (found in, e.g., 𝔓46, אi2, B, C, D, F, G, Ψ, 33, 𝔐, and the entire Latin, Syriac, and Coptic traditions) fills out and clarifies the meaning of the text, making it the less-difficult reading and therefore unlikely to be original. An early copyist, however, might easily have assumed that an original πάντας, which is masculine, referred back to the neuter term ἔθνεσιν in 3:8 but was then in the wrong gender. Under this assumption, omitting πάντας would solve the grammatical problem and clarify the text (Metzger 1994: 534). When this consideration is added to the early and geographically diverse support for the inclusion of πάντας, this seems to be the best reading, despite the hesitation of a number of experts.[25]

3:13. Some witnesses, primarily from the Alexandrian tradition (e.g., 𝔓46, C, 33, 81, 104, 436, 459, 1573, 1739, 1912, 2127), have ἡμῶν (our) rather than ὑμῶν (your) at the end of this verse. The antiquity and geographical spread of the witnesses to ὑμῶν, however, weigh heavily in its favor (e.g., א, A, B, D, F, G, Ψ, and most Byzantine manuscripts). The confusion between the two pronouns probably arose from the identical pronounciation of υ and η in later Greek (Metzger 1994: 535).





VI. Paul’s Divinely Given Task and His Suffering for the Gentiles (3:1–13)

VII. Paul Prays for His Readers’ Inner Strength and Praises the God Who Can Give It (3:14–21)

VIII. The Growth of the Church toward Unity and Maturity (4:1–16)

IX. A Reminder of How to Live as New Human Beings (4:17–5:2)


VII. Paul Prays for His Readers’ Inner Strength and Praises the God Who Can Give It (3:14–21)

Perhaps reminded by mention of his imprisonment and his readers’ discouragement (3:13), Paul now makes his way back to the intercessory prayer he had started in 3:1. In his first intercessory prayer report in 1:17–23, he had described his prayers that God might open the eyes of his readers’ hearts so they might see the “surpassing greatness” of the “power” he had made available to believers (1:19). Since then, Paul has himself helped to answer that prayer by reminding his readers of all that God has done for them. God has saved them “in Christ” from the power of sin, the devil, and the flesh (2:1–10); he has overcome their alienation from his people Israel and from himself (2:11–22); he has created them anew (2:10); he has included them as building blocks in his spiritual temple (2:19–22); and he has revealed to them the critical role they play in his age-old plan for the universe (3:10; cf. 1:9–10). The instrument of this revelation, Paul himself, is an example of God’s grace and power at work (3:2–13).

With all this behind him, Paul is now ready to launch a second intercessory prayer report, whose burden is similar to the first report. He wants his readers to know that he prays for God to strengthen them in the inner human being so that Christ might dwell in their hearts and they might become strong enough to grasp the vast dimensions of Christ’s love for them. The ultimate goal of this prayer is that his readers might “be filled up to all the fullness of God” (3:19b), that is, that they might be all God has created them as individuals (2:10) and as the church (2:15) to be (O’Brien 1999: 266).

Paul next brings the entire first half of the letter to a close with an elaborate ascription of praise to God. This doxology incorporates some of the most important themes of his intercessory prayers (3:20–21). The God who is at work in Paul and his readers is powerful enough to do more than they can even imagine. Eternal glory is his, precisely in the place where his powerful work is evident (the church) and in the person through whom he has so lavishly blessed the church (Christ Jesus).

The whole section (3:14–21) consists of two long sentences, one of eighty-six words (vv. 14–19) and one of thirty-seven words (vv. 20–21). Both sentences are characterized by a peculiar combination of structure and looseness. The intercessory prayer report (vv. 14–19) contains an introduction (vv. 14–15) and three purpose clauses (vv. 16–17, 18–19a, and 19b). The first two purpose clauses each contain a main verb followed by two explanatory infinitives, and the final purpose clause gives the climactic goal of Paul’s intercession. Yet as the exegesis below will explain, important elements of the syntax and grammar within this larger structure remain profoundly ambiguous.

The doxology follows the same pattern: it has a standard liturgical structure, but it revises and expands this structure in crucial ways to accent the themes that have consumed Paul’s attention in the letter so far. He becomes so redundant and expansive that he seems to be grasping to express the ineffable.

As we have sometimes seen elsewhere in the letter (1:4; 2:14–15a), this combination of formal structure and spontaneity probably originated in the letter’s oral composition. When Paul dictated it, he was able by the cadence of his voice to solve the syntactical problems that now face us as we pore over the text in silent study.

The intercessory prayer report and the doxology, therefore, are not mere repetitions of traditional forms, and they certainly are not scholarly literary productions. They are heartfelt prayers and examples of exactly the kind of “boldness and confident access” that believers have through faith, as Paul has just mentioned in 3:12. God is Paul’s Father, and so Paul can speak as freely as any son would speak with a father in whose love he has confidence. The mention of kneeling, the wordiness, the syntactical ambiguity, and the way that at least the intercessory prayer report unleashes “a flood of thoughts” in an intensifying crescendo (Schnackenburg 1991: 144–45) betray Paul’s emotional investment in the subjects of the prayer and those for whom he prays. The apostolic responsibility he felt for the encouragement of his readers, combined with a deeply seated conviction that they could be encouraged by the power of God and the vast love of Christ, gives the intercessory prayer report and the concluding doxology their unusual character.





VII. Paul Prays for His Readers’ Inner Strength and Praises the God Who Can Give It (3:14–21)

A. Paul Prays for His Readers’ Inner Strength (3:14–19)

B. Paul Praises the God Who Is Able to Strengthen His Readers (3:20–21)


A. Paul Prays for His Readers’ Inner Strength (3:14–19)

Paul’s concern about his readers’ discouragement (3:13) leads him to return to the theme of his intercessory prayers for them (cf. 1:17–23). Unlike the benediction in 1:3–14 and the doxology in 3:20–21, this is, precisely speaking, a prayer report rather than an actual prayer (cf. 1:15–23). Paul describes how he prays when he bows his knees before the Father on their behalf. This distinction helps to explain how Paul can, in the middle of the prayer, address his readers (“You are rooted and founded in love!”), but it would be a mistake to emphasize the distinction too heavily. The rush of the section’s eighty-six words and the ambiguity of the syntax reveal that this is more than a “report.” It is also an actual prayer for the readers.

Paul prays in order that God might, by his Spirit, give his readers strength in their inner selves to understand that Christ dwells in their hearts. He prays this so that they might be able to grasp what no human being can understand without God’s help: the vast extent of Christ’s love, a love so massive that, as the revelation of the mystery has shown, it includes “all the saints” in all their diversity (2:11–22; 3:6, 10). Grasping this truth will enable Paul’s readers to progress toward the goal of reaching “the fullness of God,” that is, of being everything God created human beings individually, and his people corporately, to be.



Exegesis and Exposition

14For this reason, I bow my knees before the Father ⌜ ⌝, 15from whom every family in the heavens and on earth is named, 16that he may grant you, according to the wealth of his glory, to be strengthened in power through his Spirit in the inner human being, 17aso that Christ might dwell through faith in your hearts—17b[You are] rooted and founded in love!—18in order that you may become strong enough to grasp with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth . . . 19aand to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, 19bin order that ⌜you might be filled⌝ up to all the fullness of ⌜God⌝.

[3:14–15] The phrase τούτου χάριν (toutou charin, for this reason) recalls the τούτου χάριν of 3:1 and signals the resumption of the prayer that Paul started but then interrupted at that point. In 3:1 the phrase pointed back to 2:19–22, with its discussion of how God has incorporated believing Gentiles, alongside believing Jews, into his people and therefore into his metaphorical dwelling place. Here the phrase recalls not only that theme but also the intervening digression that describes Paul’s personal role in assembling this ethnically unified group, a role that paradoxically brought suffering to Paul at the same time that it brought glory to the Gentiles. It is “for this reason”—in the service of this paradoxical calling—that Paul utters the intercessory prayer he is about to describe on behalf of his readers.

Paul describes the action of praying as bending his knees to the Father. The normal posture for prayer in antiquity, whether among Jews, Greeks, or Romans, was standing, although occasionally people knelt to pray.[1] Kneeling to request something from a powerful superior was common (2 Kings 1:13; 1 Chron. 29:20; Mark 1:40; Matt. 17:14; 20:20; cf. Isa. 45:23; Phil. 2:10; Rom. 14:11), and this apparently made kneeling, on occasion, an appropriate posture before God in prayer (Ps. 95:6; 1 Chron. 29:20; 2 Chron. 29:29; Acts 21:5; Dan. 6:11 Theod.). People sometimes knelt when uttering emotionally charged prayers (1 Esdr. 8:73; cf. Ezra 9:5; Luke 5:8; 22:41; Acts 7:60), and the reference to kneeling here adds to the pathos that is already present in the references to Paul’s imprisonment and sufferings (3:1, 13). Paul’s prayers for his readers are deeply heartfelt.

Paul prays to τὸν πατέρα (ton patera, the Father), a term that he uses frequently of God in Ephesians (1:2, 3, 17; 2:18; 4:6; 5:20; 6:23) and that communicates the intimacy of God’s relationship with believers. As Father, God has adopted them into his family (1:5) and made them his heirs (1:11). They are part of his household (2:19–22), and by his Spirit they may speak with him freely and without fear (2:18; 3:12). Paul speaks freely to God when he prays for his readers, so addressing him as Father is fitting.

The term πατέρα (patera) also introduces a play on the closely related word πατριά (patria) that follows it. The basic meaning of πατριά is “family” or “clan” (e.g., Num. 1:4; 1 Chron. 6; Tobit 5:12; Jdt. 8:2, 18; Josephus, Ant. 6.51; Luke 2:4), although it could be used to cover larger people groups within a nation (Ps. 21:28 [22:28 MT; 22:27 Eng.]; 1 Chron. 16:28 LXX; Acts 3:25).[2] Every family “on earth” is easy enough to understand on this definition—the expression must refer to people groups, and especially to Jews and Gentiles (cf. 2:11–13; Abbott 1897: 94). But what could “every family in the heavens” mean? It probably refers to the groupings of evil spiritual powers mentioned elsewhere in the letter: rulers, authorities, powers, dominions, and world rulers (1:21; 3:10; 6:12).

Paul prays to the Father “from whom” these social groups “are named.” Some commentators have thought that if the names of these groups originate with God, those located “in the heavens” could only be good angelic beings (Schnackenburg 1991: 310), and this has led Muddiman (2001: 167) to avoid understanding πατριά as a reference to angelic beings at all. Instead, he argues, the term refers to a “Christian household” when used of earthly families and to “departed Christians who are thought of as still organized for worship in the same way” when used of heavenly families.

It is much more likely, however, that when Paul speaks of the Father as naming the families of earth and heaven he means that God created them and demonstrated his authority over them by naming them (cf. Ps. 147:4).[3] Precisely what these names were does not matter. Paul’s point is that he prays to the one who is the Father of believers, who is the creator of the universe, and who is able to exercise authority over all he has created.

The God who created every social group, even the evil enemy powers that have such a stranglehold on “the Course of this world” (2:2), is the Father whom Paul addresses in prayer. God, then, is not only the Father to whom believers can speak freely and confidently in prayer but the Creator and the powerful authority over all social groups, including the inimical spiritual powers ranged against them (cf. Arnold 1989: 58–59).

[3:16–17a] Paul now begins to describe the substance of his prayer, but the organization of this description is ambiguous. In 3:16, 18, and 19b he uses three ἵνα (hina, that) clauses, which could indicate the three main petitions of his prayer: (1) “that” God might give his readers inward strength (vv. 16–17), (2) “that” his readers might be able to understand the magnitude of Christ’s love for them (vv. 18–19a), and (3) “that” they might be filled with the fullness of God (v. 19b). A number of interpreters think the passage has this structure (Barth 1974: 368; Arnold 1989: 86; Lincoln 1990: 197; O’Brien 1999: 253).

As we will see in the exegesis of 3:18–19a below, however, the first two ἵνα clauses are not as closely parallel to each other as some interpreters think, and as everyone recognizes, the third ἵνα clause is much shorter and has little structural similarity to the other two. In addition, if the three clauses articulated the three main petitions of the prayer, we would expect Paul to coordinate them with each other using conjunctions (“I bow my knees before the Father [praying] that . . . and that . . . and that . . .”), but these conjunctions are missing (Hoehner 2002: 485). Instead, we should think of the prayer report’s clauses as building on each other and of the prayer report itself becoming increasingly intense (Schnackenburg 1991: 144). Here in 3:16–17a, then, Paul introduces both the purpose of the prayer and its main request (Hoehner 2002: 485).[4]

The structure of this main request is also ambiguous. It begins with ἵνα δῷ (hina dō, that he might give), followed by two infinitival phrases that are roughly parallel to each other. Each has an aorist infinitive (κραταιωθῆναι, krataiōthēnai, to be strengthened; κατοικῆσαι, katoikēsai, to dwell) followed by two prepositional phrases: one beginning with διά (dia, by), describing the means by which the action of the infinitive is accomplished; and one beginning with ἐν (en, in), describing the location of the action.

The two infinitival phrases, however, are only roughly parallel. The first phrase is preceded by two additional qualifiers (κατὰ τὸ πλοῦτος τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ, kata to ploutos tēs doxēs autou, according to the wealth of his glory; δυνάμει, dynamei, in power), and the second infinitival phrase has an expressed subject (τὸν Χριστόν, ton Christon, Christ).

The parallelism between the two infinitives and the prepositional phrases that modify them may mean that they are interdependent: the second infinitive and its modifiers restate in other terms the first infinitive with its modifiers. If this is correct, then the strengthening and the dwelling are conceived of as two ways of speaking of the same action; this action happens through faith and through the Spirit, and it takes place in the inner human being, that is, the heart (Lincoln 1990: 197; Schnackenburg 1991: 145, 149; Best 1998: 341; O’Brien 1999: 258).

Two considerations make it slightly more likely, however, that the second infinitival phrase advances the prayer by supplying the result of the first infinitival phrase. First, the two qualifiers that precede the first infinitive (κατὰ τὸ πλοῦτος τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ and δυνάμει) push the second infinitive so far from the main verb, δῷ (dō, might give), that it is difficult to see how it could be dependent on that verb. It must instead be dependent on the preceding infinitive, κραταιωθῆναι. Second, if the second infinitive merely restates the first infinitive in other terms, we would expect a coordinating conjunction such as καί (kai, and) to link the two infinitives (Hoehner 2002: 480–81).

Paul, then, is asking God to give his readers strength, and he is also asking God that, as a result of this strength, Christ might dwell in his readers’ hearts (Alford 1857: 106; Ellicott 1859: 70, Eadie 1883: 246; Hoehner 2002: 481). The request for his readers “to be strengthened” (κραταιωθῆναι, krataiōthēnai) uses a term that in the LXX is frequently aligned with the inner qualities of courage (1 Sam. 4:9; 2 Sam. 10:12; Pss. 26:14 [27:14 MT, Eng.]; 30:25 [31:25 MT, Eng.]) and determination (Ruth 1:18). Paul also uses it this way in 1 Cor. 16:13: “Be on the alert, stand firm in the faith, be manly [ἀνδρίζεσθε, andrizesthe], be strong [κραταιοῦσθε, krataiousthe].”

As we just saw, he qualifies this term in four ways: two qualifiers appear before and two after κραταιωθῆναι. The two qualifiers before κραταιωθῆναι describe the resources from which this strengthening will come (κατὰ τὸ πλοῦτος τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ, kata to ploutos tēs doxēs autou, according to the wealth of his glory) and the specific respect in which Paul asks God to strengthen the letter’s readers (δυνάμει, dynamei, in power).

The first qualifier makes clear that he wants them to be strengthened according to the standard of “the wealth of [God’s] glory.” God’s “glory” could be his “brightness,” his “greatness,” or his “renown” (BDAG 256–58). The term sometimes has connotations of power, as it does in Col. 1:11, where Paul tells the Colossians that he prays for God to empower them “with all power . . . according to the might of his glory” (ἐν πάσῃ δυνάμει . . . κατὰ τὸ κράτος τῆς δόξης αὐτοῦ, en pasē dynamei . . . kata to kratos tēs doxēs autou); or in Rom. 6:4, where he says that Christ was raised from the dead “by the glory of the Father” (BDAG 257).[5]

This is certainly the connotation of δόξα here, as Paul’s second qualifier of κραταιωθῆναι makes explicit. Δυνάμει (dynamei, in power) is a “dative of respect” (BDF §197) describing the particular facet of his readers’ existence that Paul asks God to strengthen. If we put these two qualifiers together, Paul prays that God would give his readers fortitude, and do this out of the vast resources of his own majestic might.

The two qualifiers that come after κραταιωθῆναι tell the means and location of the strengthening. First, Paul prays that God would strengthen the power of the letter’s recipients διὰ τοῦ πνεύματος αὐτοῦ (dia tou pneumatos autou, through his Spirit). Paul frequently links the Spirit with power in his letters (Fee 1994: 695), sometimes to refer to the divine power that accompanies the preaching of the gospel (1 Thess. 1:5; 1 Cor. 2:4) and sometimes to refer to the Spirit’s power to effect such interior qualities as hope (Rom. 15:13) and avoiding cowardice (2 Tim. 1:7).

As the final qualifier of κραταιωθῆναι shows, Paul is concerned here with the interior life of his readers. He prays that God will strengthen them in power εἰς τὸν ἔσω ἄνθρωπον (eis ton esō anthrōpon, in the inner human being). The expression ὁ ἔσω ἄνθρωπος (or its equivalent) appears in two other places in Paul’s Letters (see Jeremias, TDNT 1:365). In 2 Cor. 4:16 he contrasts his “outer human being” that “is being destroyed” with his “inner [human being]” that is “being renewed day by day.” The contrast seems to be between Paul’s physical body, subject to pain and hardship, and his inner self (Thrall 1994: 348–51; pace Harris 2005: 359–60). Because this inner self is being renewed daily, he is not “discouraged” (ἐγκακέω, engkakeō) by the hardships he faces in his ministry (4:7–12; cf. 4:1). In Rom. 7:22–23 ὁ ἔσω ἄνθρωπος is, similarly, equivalent to the νοῦς (nous, mind).

The inner human being, then, is the interior life of the person, which God, by his Spirit, can strengthen with divine power. If Paul’s readers were discouraged (ἐγκακεῖν, enkakein) because of the suffering that the apostle was experiencing in the course of his ministry to the Gentiles (Eph. 3:13), and perhaps because they too were suffering, then Paul prays that God might give them the inner strength that in 2 Corinthians he says he himself experienced under similar circumstances.

As a result of this inner strengthening, Christ will “dwell [κατοικῆσαι, katoikēsai], through faith, in [their] hearts.” Paul does not imply by this that Christ is absent from their hearts. They could hardly be sealed by the Spirit (1:13), united with Christ in his resurrection and exaltation (2:5–6), and incorporated into the place where God dwells (κατοικητήριον, katoikētērion) by his Spirit (2:22) yet fail to have Christ dwelling in their hearts. What they apparently lack is the inner strength and encouragement they should draw from these truths.

Once again, Paul prays that they might experience in their inner lives what he says elsewhere he has experienced: “I am crucified with Christ,” he tells the Galatians; “indeed, I no longer live, but Christ lives in me; and the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me” (Gal. 2:19b–20). There is an emphasis on union with Christ’s death here that is absent from Ephesians, but otherwise the sentiment is close to Eph. 3:17a. Union with Christ by faith brings personal, inner strength that allows the believer to live in a world dominated by rebellion against God.

[3:17b] The next clause is fraught with syntactical ambiguity. To begin with, the initial prepositional phrase ἐν ἀγάπῃ (en agapē, in love) could go either with the preceding thought (“that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts in love”; Robinson 1904: 85; cf. 175) or with the participles that follow it (“rooted and founded in love”). This same phrase shows up in five other places in the letter (1:4; 4:2, 15, 16; 5:2), and, where it is possible to be definite, it always follows what it modifies (4:2, 15, 16; 5:2). This might at first seem to be decisive evidence that here Paul speaks of Christ’s dwelling in his readers’ hearts in love.

If this were correct, however, not only would the preceding clause become overloaded with prepositional phrases (“through faith,” “in your hearts,” “in love”), but also the two participles that follow the phrase would be left dangling in the air. Paul’s readers would simply be “rooted and founded,” with no indication of the way in which Paul intended for them to understand this expression (Abbott 1897: 98; Westcott 1906: 52; Barth 1974: 371; Best 1998: 342; Muddiman 2001: 169). Paul’s readers, then, are rooted and founded “in love.”

Taking ἐν ἀγάπῃ with the two participles ἐρριζωμένοι (errizōmenoi, rooted) and τεθεμελιωμένοι (tethemeliōmenoi, founded) makes them less enigmatic, but they continue to dangle syntactically. Both are nominative plurals and therefore stand on their own with no obvious connection to anything that precedes them. As plurals, we might think they refer back to the plural pronouns ὑμῖν (hymin, to you; v. 16) and ὑμῶν (hymōn, your; v. 17), but if so, they should be in the dative or the genitive case rather than the nominative. The comments of Origen show how odd the expression looked even to those who shared Paul’s native tongue. “It seems clear to me,” he says, “that these words which follow are incorrect in reference to the preceding phrase” (Heine 2002: 160; cf. Photius [Staab 1933: 617]). None of the interpretive options is ideal, and none has gained a consensus.

A few interpreters (e.g., Westcott 1906: 52; Masson 1953: 181; Hoehner 2002: 483–84) think the two participles should be taken with the next clause, as if they came after the ἵνα of 3:18 and could modify the verb ἐξισχύσητε (exischysēte, you may be able). The two clauses might then be translated “[I pray] that you, being rooted and founded in love, may be able to comprehend . . .” Although this makes good sense in English, the Greek would be very strange: it is not normal for elements that function as part of a ἵνα clause to come before the initial ἵνα.[6]

Other interpreters have given up trying to make sense of the grammar and have concluded that the use of the nominative case here is “incorrect” or “irregular” (e.g., Origen [Heine 2002: 160]; Alford 1857: 106). They then view the clause either as describing the result of Christ’s living within the believer (e.g., Ellicott 1859: 70–71) or as introducing a new petition of Paul’s prayer (e.g., Dibelius and Greeven 1953: 77; Schnackenburg 1991: 149n12; Lincoln 1990: 197).

Rather than understanding the forms as simply anomalous, however, it is probably best to see them as functioning in the same way that finite, indicative verbs function (Best 1998: 334, 342–43; cf. BDR §468n3).[7] This use of nominative participles has ample precedent elsewhere in the NT, and especially in Paul’s undisputed letters.[8] If this is correct, then the phrase is an independent, parenthetical interjection: “You are rooted and founded in love!” This is similar to the syntactically confusing outburst at the end of 2:5: “By grace you are saved!” Here too, we may hear the voice of Paul dictating the letter. There is certainly passion and eloquence, but as we might expect in a relatively ad hoc composition, not much care for syntactical precision (cf. πεφωτισμένους [pephōtismenous] in Eph. 1:18).

Why would Paul interject such a statement? He may have done so to clarify the meaning of his request that Christ would dwell in his readers’ hearts (v. 17a). As we have seen, that statement cannot imply the absence of Christ from his readers’ hearts. Perhaps to make this explicit, he interjects here that they are already “rooted and founded in love.” God has shown them his love through the death of Christ and through uniting them with his resurrection and exaltation (2:4; 3:19; 5:1–2, 25; cf. Gal. 2:20). Paul prays, then, that God will work both through the presence of his powerful Spirit in the lives of his readers and through his readers’ faith to strengthen them so that they fully comprehend the meaning of the truth that Christ dwells within their hearts.

If this correctly represents the thrust of the passage, then “love” here is not the love of believers for one another (e.g., Calvin 1965: 168; Ellicott 1859: 71; Hoehner 2002: 482–83; cf. Eph. 4:2, 15, 16; 5:2, 25, 28, 33), nor is it the love of believers for God (e.g., Origen [Heine 2002: 161]) or Christ (e.g., Eadie 1883: 249–50; cf. 6:24). It is instead God’s love, shown especially through Christ (Best 1998: 343; O’Brien 1999: 250; Eph. 3:18–19). This love is the fertile soil and solid foundation of the believer’s life in Christ.[9] It is the believer’s source of inner strength.

[3:18–19a] This next ἵνα (hina, that) clause, like the first one, features a main verb (ἐξισχύσητε, exischysēte, you may become strong enough) completed by two aorist infinitives (καταλαβέσθαι, katalabesthai, to grasp; and γνῶναι, gnōnai, to know). The similar structure of the two clauses might be a signal that they are two petitions of the prayer and that this is the second petition (Arnold 1989: 86; Lincoln 1990: 197, 207–8; cf., e.g., Gnilka 1971: 185; O’Brien 1999: 253, 260; Muddiman 2001: 170).

Two characteristics of this second clause, however, weigh against this view. First, there is a significant difference between the use of the two infinitives in each ἵνα clause. In 3:16–17, no conjunction coordinates κραταιωθῆναι (krataiōthēnai, to be strengthened) with κατοικῆσαι (katoikēsai, to dwell), and so the second infinitive builds on the first, describing its result (“to be strengthened . . . so that Christ might dwell”). Here in 3:18–19, however, the two infinitives are clearly coordinated with each other by the conjunction τέ (te, and). Second, if we remember that this text was originally dictated in order to be read aloud, it seems unlikely that Paul would place the kind of mental demand on his hearers necessary for them, simply by listening to the text, to coordinate these two distantly separated uses of ἵνα (vv. 16 and 18). Surely if he had intended for them to do this, he would have used a coordinating conjunction to aid his listeners (cf. Hoehner 2002: 485).

The ἵνα clause of 3:18–19a, then, does not start the prayer’s second request. Instead, it builds on the immediately preceding clause and gives the reason why Paul wants Christ to dwell in his readers’ hearts through faith (Ellicott 1859: 71; Eadie 1883: 250; Aletti 2001: 192, 196; Hoehner 2002: 485).

The main verb, ἐξισχύω (exischyō) can mean simply “be able” (as it does in the B [Vat.] text of Sir. 7:6), but it often has the nuance of growing in power to the point of prevailing. Thus Josephus tells us that Herod’s son Antipater, through a series of clever and unscrupulous tactics, eventually “became strong enough to bring” (ἐξίσχυσεν εἰσαγαγεῖν, exischysen eisagagein) his mother into the marriage bed that Herod’s slain favorite Mariamne once occupied (J.W. 1.451). This is an especially significant example because it not only comes from roughly the time of Paul, but it also completes the aorist verb with an aorist infinitive, just as Paul does here.[10]

The infinitive καταλαβέσθαι is from a verb that can mean “attain . . . , seize . . . , catch,” or especially in the middle voice “process information, understand, grasp” (BDAG 520; cf. Acts 4:13; 10:34; 25:25; Philo, Moses 1.278; Josephus, Ant. 8.167). Paul prays, then, that Christ will dwell in his readers’ hearts by faith so that they “become strong enough to grasp” something mentally. The picture seems to be of a struggle to prevail over ignorance or confusion, a struggle that eventually breaks through to a realization of something.

The sense of anticipation about the identity of this “something” builds as Paul lists four terms for the measurement of its size: τὸ πλάτος καὶ μῆκος καὶ ὕψος καὶ βάθος (to platos kai mēkos kai hypsos kai bathos, the breadth and length and height and depth). Clearly, the knowledge he wants his readers to grow strong enough to understand is a knowledge of something immense. But what is it? At precisely this climactic point, the line goes dead, and the result is interpretive pandemonium. A number of views have failed to gain a consensus, at least in recent times.



The oldest known view, whose earliest and most convincing proponent was Origen (Gregg 1901–2: 411–12; Heine 2002: 161–62), assigns the terms to the four points of Christ’s cross (cf., e.g., Irenaeus, Haer. 5.17.4; Gregory of Nyssa [ACCSNT 8:155–56]; Severian [Staab 1933: 311]; Augustine, Doctr. chr. 2.41; Theophylact [PG 124:1076]; cf. Schlier 1957: 173–74).[11]

“Ambrosiaster,” probably writing in the late fourth century, thought the four terms referred to the dimensions of a perfect sphere, which, in turn, stood for the perfection of the God that Paul wanted his readers to know (ACCSNT 8:155).

A set of commentators in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries believed the terms referred to the dimensions of the “Christian temple” described in 2:20–22 and that Paul wanted his readers to understand the all-encompassing nature of the church (e.g., Bengel 1860: 86; Eadie 1883: 254–55).

More recently, scholars have thought the four terms referred to the unseen dimensions or cubic shape of Christians’ heavenly “inheritance” (cf. 1:18; Rev. 21:16; Herm. Vis. 3.2.5; Schlier, TDNT 1:518; Dibelius and Greeven 1953: 77).

More recently still, some have argued that the expression is a polemical move, defining language that once implied a flawed Christology (Gnilka 1971: 188–89) or a concern with magical manipulation of the divine (Arnold 1989: 90–96) to refer instead to Christ’s love (Gnilka 1971: 189) or God’s power (Arnold 1989: 95–96).

Three suggestions stand above the fray, however, because of their longevity and wide appeal:

1. A number of ancient interpreters believed Paul was referring to the universal dimensions of “the administrative plan [οἰκονομία, oikonomia] of the mystery” he had discussed in 3:9–10 (Ephraem of Syria [Mekitharistis 1893: 149]; Theodore of Mopsuestia [Swete 1882: 161]; Theodoret, PG 82:532).[12] Recalling the language of 3:9, for example, Theodoret says that these terms refer to “the greatness of the administration [οἰκονομίας, oikonomias] that has come about . . . since these things signify greatness” (my trans.). Later advocates of this position observe the use of similar language in various religious and philosophical contexts in antiquity when the topic is divine wisdom and the human ability to comprehend it (e.g., Job 11:7–9; 38:1–40:1; Sir. 1:3; Bar. 3:24–37; 1 En. 93.12–14; Cicero, Tusc. 1.64; Corp. herm. 10.25).[13] The Paul of the undisputed letters could certainly speak in these terms, correlating the wisdom of God with the deep things of God (1 Cor. 2:7–10), and that is probably what he or the pseudonymous author of Ephesians is doing here (Schnackenburg 1991: 150–52; Bruce 1984: 327–28; cf. De Wette 1843: 126–27; Robinson 1904: 176).

This view has the merit of explaining why Paul adopts the unusual language of four measurements at this point, and it has the merit of placing the language firmly in the broader literary and theological context of Eph. 3. It is not without problems, however. As Best (1998: 345) points out, there is no exact match between the four terms used here and any religious and philosophical text from Paul’s time. As others have observed, moreover, if Paul were referring to the administration, mystery, and wisdom of God in 3:9–10, he would be reaching back into what is clearly a separate section of the letter to do so (Abbott 1897: 99; cf. Eadie 1883: 253–54; Lincoln 1990: 213). This is a problem that does not afflict the next approach.

2. Calvin (1965: 168–69) insisted that Paul’s reference is to “nothing other than the love of Christ, of which he speaks afterwards.” He is impatient with the wide variety of suggestions about the object of the measurements that already existed in his own time, particularly with Augustine’s case that Paul refers to Christ’s cross. “All this,” he says, “pleases us with its subtlety, but what has it to do with Paul’s meaning?” Later advocates of this view point out that the four measurements are sandwiched between references to love in 3:17b and 3:19a, and that precedent exists in Rom. 8:39 for the Pauline use of the terms “height” (ὕψωμα, hypsōma) and “depth” (βάθος, bathos) in a discussion of Christ’s love (Ellicott 1859: 72; Abbott 1897: 100; Lincoln 1990: 213; Best 1998: 346; O’Brien 1999: 263; Muddiman 2001: 172–73; Hoehner 2002: 488).

The parallel in Rom. 8:39, however, is far from exact: there “height” and “depth” stand opposite Christ’s love as potential threats that, as it turns out, pose no threat at all, whereas here in Eph. 3:18 the four measurements are aligned with Christ’s love as measurements of its vastness. If Paul had intended to refer only to the immensity of Christ’s love, moreover, it is difficult to know why he chose these unusual terms to do so instead of using, for example, the language of wealth that appears so frequently elsewhere (1:7, 18; 2:7; 3:8, 16; cf. Col. 2:2).

3. It seems best, then, to adopt yet another view, which is also very old. It interprets the four measurements as primarily a reference to the vastness of divine love (v. 19a) but acknowledges that also in the background of this language lies Paul’s concern with God’s administrative plan, his mystery, and his complex wisdom (vv. 9–10). This idea goes back at least as far as Chrysostom, who thought that the measurements spoke of the mystery “administered” (οἰκονομηθέν, oikonomēthen) on behalf of believers (v. 9), especially as it was visible in the extension of God’s love everywhere (v. 19a; Chrysostom, Hom. Eph., hom. 7; NPNF 13:81; PG 62:51).[14]

In more recent times several scholars have also taken this approach (Westcott 1906: 52; MacDonald 2000: 277; Aletti 2001: 196–97; cf. Alford 1857: 107).[15] They have recognized a link between the four measurements, the use of similar dimensional language to speak of God and his wisdom (Job 11:7–9; Sir. 1:3), and Paul’s talk of God’s wisdom in 3:10 (Aletti 2001: 196–97; MacDonald 2000: 277). They have also seen, however, that a concern with divine love in the immediate context (vv. 17b and 19a) means the primary reference here is to “the immense dimensions of the agapē of Christ” (Aletti 2001: 197; cf. MacDonald 2000: 277; pace Alford 1857: 107).

This understanding of the measurement language has the advantage of recognizing its affinity with wisdom concepts in Paul’s broader cultural context (e.g., Job 11:7–9; 38:1–40:1; Sir. 1:3; Bar. 3:24–37; 1 En. 93.12–14), in Ephesians itself (3:9–10), and elsewhere in Paul’s Letters (1 Cor. 2:7–10; Rom. 11:33). Yet it also recognizes that in this context Paul is primarily concerned with the magnificence of Christ’s love. Like God’s wisdom, Christ’s love is so “wide and long and high and deep” that one can mentally grasp it only through the strengthening of God’s Spirit and the indwelling of Christ himself. It is precisely for this that Paul prays (cf. 1:18–23).

That this reading of the four measurements is on the right track receives some confirmation from the phrase σὺν πᾶσιν τοῖς ἁγίοις (syn pasin tois hagiois, with all the saints). The phrase recalls the use of σύν (syn, with) language in 2:19–21 to describe the unity of Jewish and Gentile believers in the “dwelling place” of God’s Spirit (συμπολῖται, sympolitai, citizens with; συναρμολογουμένη, synarmologoumenē, joined with; συνοικοδομεῖσθε, synoikodomeisthe, you are being built together with). The “administrative plan of the mystery” (3:9) that displays “the beautifully complex wisdom of God” (3:10) is revealed in the incorporation of Jewish and Gentile believers into this one people. The vast extent of Christ’s love, then, is best comprehended “with all the saints,” in all their social variety.

Rather than providing an object for his terms of measurement, Paul begins a new clause by using the aorist infinitive γνῶναι (gnōnai, to know).[16] This term parallels the previous aorist infinitive καταλαβέσθαι (katalabesthai, to grasp), and in this context has the same meaning. The switch to γνῶναι simply allows a rhetorically effective wordplay between the verb “to know” and the noun “knowledge” (γνώσεως, gnōseōs; Aletti 2001: 197; Muddiman 2001: 173).

After the syntactical suspense built up by the list of the four measurements and their missing object, we finally learn what Paul wants God to enable his readers to grasp. He wants them to know the vast extent of Christ’s love for them (cf. Rom. 8:35, 39). Paul had himself experienced the encouragement of Christ’s love during times of inner turbulence (2 Cor. 5:13–15; cf. Rom. 8:35), and he wanted this same encouragement for his readers during their time of discouragement (Eph. 3:13). Yet like the mystery (vv. 3–5), they could not understand the massive magnitude of Christ’s love apart from God’s revelation of it to them. This is the revelation for which Paul prays.

[3:19b] The third and final ἵνα (hina, that) clause does not introduce a third petition but provides the climactic purpose toward which the rest of the prayer has been moving. The ultimate purpose of Paul’s prayer for his readers’ inner strength and increased understanding, he now says, is that they “might be filled up to [εἰς, eis] all the fullness of God.” As many commentators recognize, the preposition here cannot mean “with” but must refer to the extent of the filling and probably carries a temporal nuance (cf. 1 Thess. 2:16; 2 Cor. 4:17; 10:15).[17] Just as in 4:13 Paul speaks of arriving “at a mature man” (εἰς ἄνδρα τέλειον, eis andra teleion) and “at the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (εἰς μέτρον ἡλικίας τοῦ πληρώματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ, eis metron hēlikias tou plērōmatos tou Christou), so here he speaks of reaching God’s “fullness.”

Interpreters have explained God’s “fullness” in several different ways: his moral excellence (Eadie 1883: 258–59; cf. Chrysostom, Hom. Eph., hom. 7; NPNF 13:82), his life and power (Lincoln 1990: 214–15), or his love (Best 1998: 348; Hoehner 2002: 491). The close correspondence between this expression and 4:13, however, provides the best key to Paul’s meaning (Robinson 1904: 177). Just as in 4:13 Paul says that the saints are on the way to becoming “mature” (τέλειος, teleios) and to reaching the full stature that Christ already possesses, so here he probably means that his readers are in the process of becoming all that God created them to be (O’Brien 1999: 266). Just as God is perfect, so one day they too will be perfect.[18]

Summary

Paul prays that God, by his Spirit, would give his readers inner strength so that they could believe that Christ dwells in their hearts. This in turn will enable them to comprehend the vast extent of Christ’s love. This inner renewal, Paul prays, will take them further along the path of becoming the people that God intended “all the saints” to be.



Additional Notes

3:14. A large number of witnesses include the phrase τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ after πατέρα, including Western (e.g., D, F, G, 1912), some Alexandrian (e.g., Ψ, 104), and most Byzantine witnesses. This is significant testimony, and on the basis of its geographical diversity, Hoehner (2002: 473n1) accepts the phrase as original. The phrase does not appear in a large number of witnesses, however, including the earliest manuscripts of Ephesians (𝔓46, א, A, B). The testimony to its omission is admittedly dominated by witnesses in the Alexandrian tradition, but the antiquity of these witnesses is strong evidence that the phrase was not original. Its addition, moreover, spoils the wordplay between πατέρα and πατριά (Best 1998: 377) and is easily explicable as a scribe’s accidental expansion on the basis of familiarity with the longer expression (cf. 1:3; Rom. 15:6; 2 Cor. 11:31; Metzger 1994: 535).

3:19. Instead of ἵνα πληρωθῆτε εἰς πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τοῦ θεοῦ, some witnesses (e.g., 𝔓46, B, 0278, 462, 1175) read ἵνα πληρωθῇ πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τοῦ θεου (in order that all the fullness of God might be filled). Although this reading does have the support of the early Alexandrian manuscripts 𝔓46 and B, the evidence for reading πληρωθῆτε εἰς is much stronger. Not only are the witnesses to it early and diverse (e.g., א, A [Alexandrian]; D, F, G [Western]; K, L, P [Byzantine]), but also the reason for a change to the second option is clear: it removes the difficult εἰς, whose most obvious meaning is “into” rather than “up to.” A few late witnesses (e.g., 1881, and some Old Latin and Vulgate manuscripts) read ἵνα πληρωθῆτε εἰς πᾶν τὸ πλήρωμα τοῦ Χριστοῦ (in order that you might be filled up to all the fullness of Christ). Although this reading has no claim to authenticity, it probably derives from a correct interpretive instinct to read the difficult εἰς in this text through the lens of εἰς in 4:13 and 4:15.





VII. Paul Prays for His Readers’ Inner Strength and Praises the God Who Can Give It (3:14–21)

A. Paul Prays for His Readers’ Inner Strength (3:14–19)

B. Paul Praises the God Who Is Able to Strengthen His Readers (3:20–21)


B. Paul Praises the God Who Is Able to Strengthen His Readers (3:20–21)

When Paul prays for his readers, his requests are not small. The goal of his prayer is that his readers, now discouraged (3:13), will eventually comprehend what is humanly impossible to understand and that this understanding will lead them to become all that God has created them to be (3:14–19). He now follows the report that this is how he prays with an actual prayer of praise to the God who is able to do the unimaginable and who is at work, with this great power, in believers. Believers make up the church, and God has created and richly blessed them “in Christ,” so Paul appropriately says that God receives glory “in the church” and “in Christ Jesus.” The expansiveness of his praise shows that he is reaching to express the ineffable, and at least once, his Greek becomes nearly untranslatable. The phrase ὑπὲρ πάντα . . . ὑπερεκπερισσοῦ ὧν αἰτούμεθα ἢ νοοῦμεν (hyper panta . . . hyperekperissou hōn aitoumetha ē nooumen) can perhaps be rendered “beyond everything, infinitely more than what we ask or imagine” (v. 20).

This doxology is a fitting conclusion not only to Paul’s intercessory prayer report but also to the entire first half of the letter. Paul has begun with a benedictory prayer (1:3–14), expressing praise to God almost entirely in the first-person plural (1:3–12), and now he ends this first major portion of his letter with another first-person expression of praise to God. Both prayers comprise lengthy sentences, are redundant, and reveal a mixture of adherence to form and spontaneity. The two prayers, then, fittingly bracket the letter’s first half with its concern for God’s gracious power made effective for the church.



Exegesis and Exposition

20Now to the One who is able to do ⌜beyond⌝ everything, infinitely more than what we ask or imagine, according to the power at work in us, 21to him be the glory ⌜in the church and in Christ Jesus⌝ for all the generations of the age of the ages. Amen.

[3:20] Paul brings the first major section of his letter to a close with a liturgical form that has often been called a doxology.[1] Doxologies are expressions of praise to God that speak of his glory, honor, or might. They appear in the OT as part of temple worship (1 Chron. 16:28–29; Pss. 29:1–2; 96:7) and also show up occasionally in the literature of Hellenistic Jewish piety (e.g., Pr. Man. 15 [Odes 12:15 LXX]; 4 Macc. 18:24). They became common in early Christian literature, where they tend to occur at the end of a section (e.g., 1 Pet. 4:11; 1 Clem. 20.12; 58.2; Mart. Pol. 21; 22) or near the end of a document (e.g., 1 Pet. 5:11; Heb. 13:21; 1 Clem. 64; Mart. Pol. 20.2). Paul frequently uses doxologies to conclude a section of a letter (Gal. 1:5; Phil. 4:20; Rom. 11:36; 1 Tim. 1:17; 2 Tim. 4:18). Once he places a doxology near the end of a letter (1 Tim. 6:16), and once, if Rom. 16:25–27 is genuine, at the very end (cf. Pr. Man. 15; 4 Macc. 18:24).

Hellenistic Jewish and Christian doxologies tend to follow a four-part pattern (Aune 1997: 44): (1) a reference to the one who receives the glory, (2) a reference to the glory itself, (3) a reference to the eternal duration of the glory, and (4) the term “amen.” Paul’s doxology in Eph. 3:20–21 has all four parts.

First, ancient doxologies begin with a reference to God or Christ,[2] often using a pronoun, and this reference is almost always in the dative case.[3] When the reference includes the article, the article is often followed by δέ (de, now), signaling that the doxology comprises a new segment of the discourse.[4]

In verse 20 Paul follows the form that opens the doxology with a dative-case articular expression and δέ. The doxology, then, clearly forms a new segment of the discourse, and the function of this new segment, as with Rom. 11:36, is to draw a major portion of the letter to a close.[5] Paul begins his doxology by ascribing glory τῷ . . . δυναμένῳ (tō . . . dynamenō, to the one who is able).

This same description of God appears in doxologies in Jude 24–25 and Mart. Pol. 20.2, but it would be a major mistake to conclude from this that it is merely a formal or traditional feature that Paul unthinkingly takes over at this point. The availability of God’s power to believers has been a prominent theme in the letter so far. Paul has prayed for his readers to understand “the surpassing greatness of his power [δύναμις, dynamis] for us who believe” (1:19). He has then shown how God has used the same great power that raised Christ from the dead and seated him at God’s right hand to unify believers with the victorious Christ and give them victory over evil powers as well (1:20–2:10). Despite his position as the least of all the saints, Paul’s own historically crucial ministry to the Gentiles is also a demonstration of “the effect of his power [δύναμις, dynamis]” (3:7–8). He has just described his prayer that God would strengthen his readers “in power [δύναμις]” so they might grow strong enough to grasp Christ’s love for them (3:16, 18–19). When Paul addresses God as ὁ δυνάμενος (ho dynamenos, the one who is able), then, he draws these threads together: God is the one who is powerful, and he has placed his power at the disposal of Paul’s readers.

Paul expands this description of God in two ways.[6] First, the title ὁ δυνάμενος needs a complementary infinitive; elsewhere in doxologies that use this title, the infinitive specifies what God is able to do (e.g., φυλάξαι, phylaxai, to guard; στῆσαι, stēsai, to cause to stand [Jude 24]; στηρίξαι, stērixai, to strengthen [Rom. 16:25]; εἰσαγαγεῖν, eisagagein, to lead into [Mart. Pol. 20.2]). Here, however, in a way that is fully consistent with the tone of Ephesians, Paul complements the title with a general and expansive expression: God is able “to do” (ποιῆσαι, poiēsai) not some specific task, and not even anything he and his readers can ask or imagine, but ὑπὲρ πάντα . . . ὑπερεκπερισσοῦ ὧν (hyper panta . . . hyperekperissou hōn, beyond everything . . . infinitely more than what) they can “ask or imagine.”

The preposition ὑπέρ in the phrase ὑπὲρ πάντα means “over and above, beyond, more than” (cf., e.g., 1 Cor. 10:13; Philem. 21; BDAG 1031), and it is followed, redundantly, with the rare term ὑπερεκπερισσοῦ. This word appears here and twice in 1 Thessalonians (3:10; 5:13) for the first time in all known Greek literature. Apart from allusions to these texts, it seldom occurs for centuries thereafter (e.g., Epiphanius, Pan. 2.387, l. 8).[7] It is composed of two elements, ὑπέρ (hyper), which appears again with the meaning “over and above,” and the phrase ἐκ περισσοῦ (ek perissou), which means “extremely” (Dan. 3:22 Theod.; Mark 6:51; Dio Chrysostom, Or. 31.64 [ἐκ περιττοῦ]; BDAG 298). The translation “infinitely more than” (BDAG 1033) captures the idea that the word communicates. Paul ascribes glory to the God who is able to do not merely what Paul and his readers ask but extremely far beyond what they can imagine. This is a fitting description of the God who has graciously made known the mystery of his administrative plan for the universe to Paul and his readers and has included them both individually and as a people in this plan. It also assures Paul’s readers that although Paul wants them to have an inner strength to understand Christ’s vast love that no one could possess on the basis of mere human ability, God is able to give it to them (Bruce 1961: 70).[8]

Second, Paul expands his description of the God “who is able” with an adverbial prepositional phrase that identifies the norm or standard against which his ability is measured. He is able κατὰ τὴν δύναμιν τὴν ἐνεργουμένην ἐν ἡμῖν (kata tēn dynamin tēn energoumenēn en hēmin, according to the power at work in us). The term δύναμιν (dynamin, power) is simply the noun form of the participle δυναμένῳ (dynamenō, who is able), and so introduces a wordplay difficult to reproduce in English translation: “the one who is able . . . according to the ability at work in us” does not capture the nuance of the terms very well but does reproduce the rhetorical effect of the expression. In his first intercessory prayer report (1:19) Paul has also said that God puts his power into effect “for us who believe” and does this κατὰ τὴν ἐνέργειαν τοῦ κράτους τῆς ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ (kata tēn energeian tou kratous tēs ischyos autou, according to the effect of the might of his strength). Since then we have learned that God does this “through his Spirit” and in “the inner human being” (3:16), and Paul is probably thinking of God’s power at work in believers in terms of the Spirit here also (Fee 1994: 697–98).

The burden of Paul’s two intercessory prayer reports (1:17–23 and 3:14–19) is that his readers might understand both the greatness of God’s power and the availability of that power to them (cf. Phil. 4:13; Col. 1:29). The first element of his concluding doxology skillfully sums up both truths by speaking of God both as one who is able to do infinitely more than we can imagine and as one who is at work within believers.

[3:21] The second element of early Christian doxologies assigns glory to God, often along with attributes such as honor, magnificence, and especially power (Deichgräber 1967: 28). Usually no explicit verb links God with these attributes, and so the understood verb could be optative (εἴη, eiē, may glory be yours), imperative (ἔστω, estō, let glory be yours), or indicative (ἐστίν, estin, glory is yours). All three moods appear in ancient doxologies when the verb is expressed, although the optative and indicative are the most likely options (Deichgräber 1967: 32). Commentators disagree about which mood is assumed here,[9] but Deichgräber (1967: 32) is surely correct in his assessment that it hardly matters: the person who expresses the wish that God should be praised is, at the same time, fulfilling that wish.[10]

Paul expands this second element of the doxology with a description of where glory is ascribed to God. Glory belongs to God “in the church and [καί, kai] in Christ Jesus.” The church makes God’s glory known because its very existence as a multiethnic community that is reconciled to God testifies to God’s beautifully complex wisdom (3:10; cf. 2:11–22). Elsewhere in Paul, Christ has glory and is himself the image of God (2 Cor. 4:4; cf. 2 Cor. 3:18; Best 1998: 351), but here at the end of Eph. 1–3, and directly after mentioning that God’s glory is present in the church, he is probably thinking especially of the close relationship between the church and Christ as the means by which God’s glory becomes visible. The church is Christ’s body, and God has given Christ, as head over all things, to the church (1:22–23). Christ is the one “in” whom the church exists as a people at peace with itself and with God (2:13–22; 3:6), and God put into effect “in Christ Jesus our Lord” his plan to make this beautifully complex wisdom known through the church (3:10).

There is no thought here of the church as equal to Christ or prior to Christ in importance. Paul is clear elsewhere that Christ is the head over all things, including the church (1:22–23; 5:23), but here the emphasis lies on the unity of Christ and the church, something Paul also emphasizes in Ephesians (1:23; 5:30–31). The plan of God for the unification of the universe revolves around the church and Christ and their close relationship with each other. It is fitting, then, for Paul to say that God is glorified in both.

The third element of early Christian doxologies is an expression for time, indicating that God’s glory will exist forever.[11] Here Paul formulates this element in an unusual way, apparently combining the more common expressions “for all the generations of the age” (Tob. 1:4; 13:12; 14:5; cf. Exod. 12:14) and “for the ages of the ages” (e.g., LXX Ps. 83:5 [84:5 MT; 84:4 Eng.]; 4 Macc. 18:24; Gal. 1:5; Phil. 4:20; 1 Tim. 1:17; 2 Tim. 4:18) to produce the verbose phrase “for all the generations of the age of the ages” (εἰς πάσας τὰς γενεὰς τοῦ αἰῶνος τῶν αἰώνων, eis pasas tas geneas tou aiōnos tōn aiōnōn; Lincoln 1990: 217).

It is possible that this is simply a rhetorically impressive way of saying “forever” and “should not be analyzed too precisely” (Lincoln 1990: 218; cf. Abbott 1897: 104). When we divide the phrase into its constituent parts, however, it is fully coherent: it describes a single age (τοῦ αἰῶνος, tou aiōnos) that consists both of a series of ages (τῶν αἰώνων, tōn aiōnōn) and of all generations (πάσας τὰς γενεὰς, pasas tas geneas). As one generation yields to another, and as one age passes to the next, for all time God will have glory both in the church and in Christ Jesus.

The fourth component of the doxology form is the concluding ἀμήν (amēn, amen), an element that derives from the use of the doxology in corporate worship (cf. Ps. 106:48; 1 Chron. 16:36; Neh. 8:6; 1QS 1.18–20; see HALOT 1:64; and cf. Delling 1962: 64). At least by the time of those who translated the Psalms into Greek, the word meant “may it be so” (γένοιτο, genoito; Pss. 40:14 LXX [41:14 MT; 41:13 Eng.]; 71:19 LXX [72:19 MT, Eng.]; 88:53 LXX [89:53 MT; 89:52 Eng.]) and was the means by which the worshiping congregation indicated that the praise of God uttered by others in worship was also the expression of their own heart (cf. 1 Cor. 14:16; Rev. 5:13–14; Delling 1962: 64).

There is no need to think, however, that Paul’s use of the term in 3:21 means that the apostle expected the congregations of western Asia to respond with “Amen” at this point in the oral reading of the letter (pace Bruce 1984: 331; Schackenburg 1991: 157; O’Brien 1999: 269). They certainly may have done this, but the “amen” here, like the “amen” in similar contexts elsewhere in Paul’s Letters, is his own final, heartfelt expression that what he has said is true.[12] Paul firmly believed that the God who was powerful enough to bless his people with every spiritual blessing, to save them from the power of sin and the devil and the flesh, to reconcile them to one another and to himself, to employ them strategically in his age-old plan for the universe, to reveal this plan to them, and to strengthen their downcast inner selves with a knowledge of the vast expanse of Christ’s love for them—this God would receive glory forever in the church that he had created, and in the Christ through whom he had created it.

Summary

Paul concludes the first major section of his letter with a doxology that praises the God who is able to accomplish what Paul desires for the letter’s readers. God’s power is immense, and he has made that power available to the church through the relationship that the church has with Christ Jesus. God’s power works “in” the church by giving it resurrection life, victory over God’s enemies, unity across ethnic lines, and peace with himself. God’s power also works within the church by means of God’s Spirit and the indwelling Christ, who encourages the church through helping it to understand the immensity of his grace. The God who is able to do all this—and much more—for the church is the God whom Paul praises, and when the church understands all that God has done for it in Christ Jesus, it too will praise God forever.



Additional Notes

3:20. The preposition ὑπέρ is missing in 𝔓46, D, F, G, and a few other witnesses. The geographical spread of the omission is interesting—it is found in a major Alexandrian witness as well as the three major Western witnesses—but the diversity and antiquity of the text with ὑπέρ (e.g., א, A, B, C, Ivid, Ψ, and most Byzantine manuscripts) weigh heavily in its favor. A scribe probably dropped ὑπέρ to make the syntax simpler and the expression less redundant (Metzger 1994: 536; Lincoln 1990: 197; Best 1998: 349).

3:21. Mention of the church before Christ Jesus apparently created theological problems for some ancient scribes who copied the text, and some of them dropped the καί (the majority reading) or switched the order (D, F, G). Either way the implication that Christ is equal to the church is erased: either he comes before and is therefore superior to the church (“in Christ Jesus and in the church”) or the church is defined by him (“in the church in Christ Jesus”). The oldest and best manuscripts (𝔓46, א, A, B, C, 0278, 6, 33, 81) have the καί and the more difficult order, however, and so this is the much more likely reading (see the full discussion in Barth 1974: 375).





VII. Paul Prays for His Readers’ Inner Strength and Praises the God Who Can Give It (3:14–21)

VIII. The Growth of the Church toward Unity and Maturity (4:1–16)

IX. A Reminder of How to Live as New Human Beings (4:17–5:2)

X. Avoiding and Transforming the Deeds of Darkness (5:3–14)


VIII. The Growth of the Church toward Unity and Maturity (4:1–16)

Paul opens chapters 4–6, the second major part of his letter, with a paragraph whose focus on unity links the two major parts together. In chapters 1–3 he has explained that his readers play an important part in God’s plan to sum up everything in heaven and on earth in Christ (1:10). The unity of the church across ethnic lines (2:11–22) accomplishes two critical elements of this plan. First, it restores the original unity of God’s creation: in Christ, Jews and Gentiles form “one new human being” (2:15). Second, it reveals the complex beauty of God’s wisdom to the inimical spiritual powers of the universe (3:10).

This “one new human being,” however, is not yet complete. When Paul changes the metaphor to that of a temple, he explains that his readers are part of a divine dwelling place that is currently under construction: they are “being joined together,” “[growing] into a holy temple in the Lord” and “being built together into the dwelling place of God” (2:21–22). In the second half of the letter, Paul will show his readers in practical ways how they can live in unity with one another and therefore fulfill the role that God has assigned them in the universe. In 4:1–16 Paul introduces these practical admonitions.

The section can be divided into two main subsections. In the first subsection (vv. 1–6) Paul launches a series of general but practical ethical admonitions based on the understanding of the church that he has developed in chapters 1–3. Paul’s readers have been called to be a new, unified people, the initial stage of God’s new creation (v. 1). Although the scope of this vision spans the universe, it is accomplished through the cultivation of such mundane qualities as humility, patience, and lovingly putting up with the foibles of others (v. 2). Paul’s readers should zealously pursue “unity” (v. 3).

We are prepared for some further practical explanation of what this means, but apparently prompted by his mention of unity, Paul instead breaks off his practical admonitions to give seven affirmations of the theological unity on which the church’s practical unity is based (vv. 4–6). The highly rhetorical—almost poetic—language that Paul uses has led a number of scholars to conclude that this section is derived from a traditional liturgy, perhaps used in a baptismal rite, but as the notes below explain, it is more likely that this is Paul’s own freely composed oratory. He does not return to the sort of practical, first-person singular, authoritative ethical instruction of 4:2–3 again until 4:17. As we have found at several other sections of the letter, then, the structure of the argument exhibits signs of a skillful organizational plan on the large scale, but also of spontaneous, probably oral, composition.

In the second subsection (vv. 7–16) Paul continues to lay the theological foundation for the church’s practical efforts at unity. Whereas the first subsection had reached its climax with an affirmation of the unity and pervasive presence of God (v. 6), this second subsection grounds the unity of the church in the work of Christ. It skillfully uses the number “one,” so prominent in 4:4–6, to shift the thought from the unity of the church and God to the importance of “each one” of God’s people in moving the church toward this unity. In the first part of this section, Paul appeals to a heavily modified form of Ps. 67:19 LXX (68:19 MT; 68:18 Eng.) to support the idea that the very Christ whose ascent to heaven and descent to hades shows him to be victorious over the inimical spiritual powers of the cosmos is the Christ who has given gifts to each believer for building up the church. The gifts of some are intended for the equipping of others to do the work of ministry, but in each case Christ has measured out the appropriate amount of “grace” for the “activity” assigned to each believer. As each believer lovingly supplies the body with what it needs to grow, it matures into the “man” God intended it to be. This “man,” as it turns out, is Christ himself, who fills the whole universe.

In 4:1–16 a number of scholars have found evidence that the letter was written in a post-Pauline environment. Two aspects of the passage are particularly important to this approach.

First, the passage seems to be heavily indebted to the language of other Pauline letters. The language of 4:1 is particularly close to 1 Thess. 4:1 and Rom. 12:1 (cf. also 1 Thess. 2:11–12). There is a similarly close correspondence between Eph. 4:1–6 and Col. 3:12–15, and between Eph. 4:16 and Col. 2:19.
