In these instances the language is so close that it appears to many interpreters that the author of Ephesians has derived his own language from these other Pauline passages (e.g., Lincoln 1990: 226–28, 230–31; Schnackenburg 1991: 173–74; Pokorný 1992: 159; MacDonald 2000: 295).

The discussion of the role of variously gifted individuals within the church in 4:7–16, moreover, recalls the similar discussions in 1 Cor. 12:4–31 and Rom. 12:3–8. In all three passages gifts are given to the “body,” and gifted Christians are urged to work together for the body’s unity. The differences between Eph. 4:7–16 and the other two passages, however, are significant (Lincoln 1990: 230):



Christ gives the gifts (Eph. 4:7–8, 11) rather than God or the Spirit (1 Cor. 12:4–11, 28; Rom. 12:3).

The “gifts” are δόματα (domata; Eph. 4:8) rather than χαρίσματα (charismata), as in the other two passages (1 Cor. 12:4, 31; Rom. 12:6).

Only five gifts are mentioned, and two of these, “evangelists and pastors,” appear in none of the other lists (Eph. 4:11).

Christ is the “head” of the body (Eph. 4:15) rather than the body itself (1 Cor. 12:12, 27; cf. Rom. 12:5).

Second, it is argued, the concerns of the author, reflected especially in the way he has nuanced the “gift” passages in the undisputed Paulines, fit best in a period after the apostle’s death when “the charism associated with leadership in Paul’s churches is apparently being routinized; it is becoming attached to an established teaching leadership” (MacDonald 2000: 299; cf. 1988: 135–36). The gifts given to the church are now narrowed to the five teaching offices listed in 4:11. Talk of the Spirit falls away and is replaced with the picture of an exalted Christ who authoritatively institutes these offices (Merklein 1973: 77–81; Zimmermann 1988: 114–15; Schnackenburg 1991: 180). Apostles lie in the past, and although prophets may continue to function in the author’s community, the author is primarily interested in the foundational role of the prophets of a bygone age. The work of these now-foundational apostles and prophets continues, however, with the evangelists, pastors, and teachers (Schnackenburg 1991: 180–81; MacDonald 2000: 299). According to Zimmermann (1988: 116–17), even the Pauline category of “teachers” is beginning to diminish in importance as they are absorbed into the category of “pastors.” The catalyst for these changes is the need to protect the church against disunity in the period after the charismatic leader Paul has passed from the scene and new waves of false teaching and persecution are washing over it (MacDonald 1988: 133, 135; 2000: 298).

This picture of Ephesians has considerable explanatory power, and its wide influence is understandable. It is heavily dependent, however, on a web of exegetical and historical decisions with several weak connections. Exegetically, it rests on a reading of 4:11 and 4:16 that is grammatically, lexically, and contextually improbable, as the exegesis below tries to show.

Historically, it adopts a model for the development of church structure that seems smoother than the complex realities reflected in early Christian literature will allow. Already in the mid-first century the indisputably authentic Paul can refer to “the instructor” (ὁ κατηχούμενος, ho katēchoumenos) as a paid class of believers who teach the Christian message (Gal. 6:6; Longenecker 1990: 279). In the late-first-century Didache (15.1–2), “prophets” and “teachers” labor alongside “bishops” and “deacons” and, confusingly, seem to do similar work. In the early second century, Ignatius assumes a highly structured threefold ministry with a single “bishop” at the top and “elders” and “deacons” taking lower positions under him (Pol. 6.1). In the mid-second century, however, Justin Martyr (1 Apol. 65; 67) reverts to the less-complex structure of a “ruler” (προεστώς, proestōs) assisted by “deacons.”[1] As if this is not enough, in his comments on Eph. 4:11 (Heine 2002: 175), Origen entertains the possibility of miracle-working “apostles” in his own time, the mid-third century.

In the first two centuries there is clearly a general trend toward a more-authoritarian structure than we see in the undisputed Paulines. A plurality of leaders seems to sit at the top of Paul’s congregational structure (1 Thess. 5:12; Phil. 1:1), whereas Justin speaks of only one “ruler” over each assembly. The situation is too complex and too conditioned by the specific circumstances of each writer, however, to draw conclusions about the date of a text from a given structure. The focus in 4:11 on gifts that preserve the apostolic tradition and stress the importance of teaching may merely reflect Paul’s awareness that false teaching has become a problem in the churches of Asia (cf. 4:14; cf. Col. 2:8, 16–23).
